utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Up first will be the City Council's nomination of Martha King for the appointment by the Council as a member of the New York City Board of Corrections.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: King to come to the witness table.

chapters.summary: Chair Ung explains the Board of Correction's Charter Section 626 duties: inspecting DOC facilities, evaluating DOC performance, setting minimum standards, handling grievances, and investigating deaths in custody. King would serve the remainder of a term ending February 1, 2029.
chapters.title: Chair Ung explains Board of Correction duties and term

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The Border Corrections is established by Section 626 of the New York City Charter is responsible for the inspection of all institutions and facilities under the jurisdiction of the Department of Corrections and of all records retained by DOC and its work.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: In addition, the Border Corrections is responsible for the evaluation of the Department of Corrections'performance.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The BOC must establish minimal standards for the care, custody, correction, treatment, supervision, and discipline of all persons held or confined under the jurisdiction of the department.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And it promulgates such minimal standards and rules and regulations after giving the mayor and commissioner an opportunity to review and comment on the proposed standards or amendments or additions to such standards.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The BOC has nine members appointed equally by the mayor, the council, and the mayor from judicial nominations.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Mayors, sorry, members serve six-year terms and vacancies are filled for the remainder of the term.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The BOC is required to establish procedures for the hearing of grievances, complaints, or requests for assistance by or on behalf of any person held or confined under the jurisdiction of the department or by any employee of the department.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The BOC must issue a report at least every three years on the department's grievance process, incorporating feedback from incarcerated individuals and recommendations for improvement, including for vulnerable population.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: This report must be submitted.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: to the council and post on the board's website.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The BOC is also in most instances obligated to investigate and prepare a report about the death of any individual in DOC custody.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The report should include any recommendations about the measures DOC or correctional health services may implement in the future to prevent the circumstances that contribute to individual's death.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Such reports should be posted on the board's website along with any response from DOC or correctional health services.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: If appointed to the BOC, Martha King will serve the remainder of the six-year term that ends on February 1, 2029.

chapters.summary: Chair Ung introduces Martha King as Program Director for Education and Urban Affairs at the Charles H. Revson Foundation. King was BOC Executive Director from 2015 to 2019, oversaw a sexual abuse prevention regulation, injury monitoring, and data transparency, and previously worked in the Office of the First Deputy Mayor.
chapters.title: Chair Ung introduces Martha King's background

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: We are joined today by Martha King, who currently serves as the Program Director for Education and Urban Affairs at Charles H.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Revson Foundation.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: From 2015 to 2019, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: King served as Executive Director of the Board of Corrections, where she oversaw the development of the board's first sexual abuse prevention regulation in 25 years.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Established in a public monitoring system for injuries sustained by individuals in custody, advanced data transparency initiatives, and advised the Council on legislation related to the Board's oversight responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Prior to that, she served as Senior Policy Analyst in the Office of the First Deputy Mayor, also served as an independent consultant to numerous not-for-profit organizations.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: King holds a Juris Doctorate degree in Sociology from the Graduate Center at the City University of New York, as well as two master's degrees from Princeton University, one in Public Affairs and one in Urban and Regional Planning.

chapters.summary: Committee counsel asks Martha King to raise her right hand and affirm that she will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before the committee.
chapters.title: Committee counsel administers affirmation to Martha King

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I now recognize the committee council to administer the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please raise your right hand.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth in your statements before this committee and in response to all questions posed by council members?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I do.

chapters.summary: Chair Ung greets Martha King and recognizes her to make an opening statement.
chapters.title: Chair Ung invites Martha King to give opening statement

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: King.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I recognize you now to make an opening statement.

chapters.summary: Martha King thanks the committee and describes her family's move to New York so her father could run the Montefiore Rikers Island Health Service. She calls herself a philanthropic advisor and strategist with 25 years across foundation, government, and nonprofit sectors.
chapters.title: Martha King describes her background and connection to Rikers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Ung and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: It's an honor to be here today and to be considered for appointment to the New York City Board of Correction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: My connection to New York City and in an unusual way to Rikers Island began when I was a few months old and my parents moved our family to Chicago, to New York, so that my father could run

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: the Montufior Rikers Island Health Service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: This move made me a New Yorker and created a lifelong commitment to public service and improving the institutions, particularly those of the criminal justice system that shape life in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I'm now a philanthropic advisor and strategist with 25 years experience working across the foundation, government, and nonprofit sectors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I've spent my career seeking to better New York City and have familiarity with diverse policy areas.

chapters.summary: King recounts serving as BOC Executive Director from 2015 to 2019, when the agency's staff and budget more than doubled and monitoring, investigations, research, regulations, and public reporting expanded. She remains involved through a national network and as chair of the Correctional Association of New York's board.
chapters.title: Martha King recounts BOC executive director tenure

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: From 2015 through 2019, I had the privilege of serving as executive director of the Board of Correction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: During that period, with support from the council and the mayor's office, we increased the agency's staff and budget by more than double and significantly expanded its monitoring, investigations, research,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: regulations and public reporting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Since that time, I have remained involved in oversight of jails and prisons through a national network, my research, public engagements, and serving as chair of the Correctional Association of New York's Board of Directors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: This experience gives me deep appreciation for what independent oversight can accomplish

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: and an awareness of its limitations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I have firsthand understanding of the obligations and responsibilities of BOC members and would welcome the opportunity to uphold them.

chapters.summary: King says BOC institutional knowledge, real-time insights, and transparency are especially important during intensive court oversight and the transition to borough-based jails. She quotes David Dinkins on demeaning jail conditions and the presumption of innocence.
chapters.title: Martha King on BOC's role amid court oversight and borough jails

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: At a time of intensive court oversight and the significant transition to borough-based jails, the BOC's institutional knowledge

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: on the ground and real-time insights and commitment to transparency are especially important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: The BOC has a remarkable history of reforming the city's jails and establishing the elements of safer conditions, including access to the courts and legal services, visits, daily showers, the practice of religion, health and mental health care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: In 1977, future Mayor David Dinkins testified before the Board of Correction encouraging its regulations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: He noted, quote, we have abandoned the presumption of innocence when we allow such demeaning and debasing conditions in our jails to exist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: The BOC's regulations remain a bulwark against demeaning and debasing conditions, even as those may shift in nature.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Mayor Dinkins'statement holds true today, and improving conditions

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: in city jails and upholding the presumption of innocence must be a priority for our city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Three quarters of the people detained on Rikers returned directly straight to our communities.

chapters.summary: King notes that three-quarters of people detained on Rikers return directly to their communities. If appointed, she promises to visit jails regularly, follow the facts, exercise independent judgment, and continue the Council-BOC reform legacy.
chapters.title: Martha King commits to independent jail oversight

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: If appointed, I would bring deep knowledge of the city's jail system and a strong commitment to New York City to the board.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I would also advance the work with an open mind, digging into current conditions and evaluating the evidence before the board today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I would visit the jails regularly, work with other board members and staff to set priorities, follow the facts, and exercise independent judgment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: The council has a long history of appointing dedicated independent members of the board and of partnering with the BOC to implement reforms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: It would be an honor and privilege to further that legacy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to appear and for your consideration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And I look forward to your questions.

chapters.summary: Chair Ung thanks King, notes Councilmember Riley has joined, and asks why King wants to serve on the Board of Correction. King cites a promising reform moment with DOC leadership, federal court intervention, borough-based jails, and BOC's transparency role.
chapters.title: Chair Ung asks Martha King why she wants to serve on BOC

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: We've also been joined by Councilmember Raleigh.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So first I'm going to kick it off asking some questions, then I'm going to pass it up to my council members and I'll probably come back.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So first, why do you want to serve on the Board of Corrections?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Well, I think we have an especially promising moment to create fundamental reform in the jails, considering the current leadership

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: of the Department of Correction, considering the federal court's intervention, and considering the move to the borough-based jails.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: The board's standards and regulations, its institutional and historical knowledge and memory are crucial to that process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Additionally, the board is the one agency among all of those involved in reform of the jails that's

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: formally committed to transparency and to speaking with all parties, combining real-time data and conversations with people on staff and people in custody.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Ung asks King about her most significant reforms as BOC Executive Director. King highlights doubling the budget and staff, more investigations and public reporting, and the first two comprehensive grievance system evaluations, which led to Council legislation and a new digital complaint system.
chapters.title: Chair Ung asks King about reforms as BOC executive director

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: You previously served as the BLC as executive director.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: What are the most significant reforms that you led during your service and what impacts did they have?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I'm very proud that when I was executive director working with the council and the mayor's office, we were able to more than double the budget and the staff, which translated to more investigations, more public reporting,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: additional regulations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: and much more transparency in our city's jail system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: One or two examples of which I'm particularly proud of were the work by the board to evaluate the Department of Corrections complaint and grievance system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: We issued the first two comprehensive evaluations of the grievance system when I was executive director.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And those evaluations led to a package of city council legislation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: It also led to an entirely new digital centralized complaint system run by the Department of Correction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: It allowed them to streamline all of their 311 complaints with other mechanisms for getting complaints.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And it also led to staffing and policy changes that improved the grievance system.

chapters.summary: Chair Ung asks what role incarceration should play in the criminal justice system. King says incarceration has a necessary but limited role for public safety and legal process, that the country overuses it, and that New York City has reduced incarceration while also reducing crime.
chapters.title: Chair Ung asks King about the role of incarceration

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Based on your experience overseeing the city jails, what role do you believe incarceration should play in the criminal justice system?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Well, I believe incarceration has a necessary but limited role.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So it should be used when it is necessary to protect public safety, to protect the integrity of the legal process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I think we have history and a record in this country of overusing incarceration to try to solve problems that cannot be solved with a jail or with a prison.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: We also have a record in New York City over the past 30 years or since Mayor Dinkins.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Of reducing the number of people who are incarcerated while we've all

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: also reduced crime and made the city safer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So I hope that we can continue to build on that trajectory.

chapters.summary: Chair Ung asks what lessons King would bring from chairing the Correctional Association of New York. King clarifies that the Association monitors state prisons, says she consulted the Conflicts of Interest Board, and emphasizes using data and focusing on implementation integrity.
chapters.title: Chair Ung asks King about lessons from Correctional Association

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: You currently serve as the chair of the Correctional Association of New York.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: What lessons from that role will you bring to the Board of Corrections?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So just to clarify, so in case anyone's confused, the Correctional Association monitors and oversees the state prison system, entirely different jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And I did talk to the Conflicts of Interest Board, and I will be cognizant of any potential conflicts if I were to be appointed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I was not advised of any by the COIB.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So I think with Canny's experience, my experience at Canny and at the Board of Correction, one of the key lessons is using data to inform our conversations about

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: potential policy changes and also paying attention to the actual implementation of reforms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Prisons and jails have many, many policies and regulations that they're supposed to be following.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: The problem lies in the implementation and integrity of those policies and regulations on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And so I believe that my lessons from Canny and the board previously are to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: really be persistent and consistent in looking at implementation and conditions in real time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: and using data from all sides.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So as much data as can be gathered through information systems and data that comes from people who working in the system or are detained in the system bring important perspectives.

chapters.summary: Chair Ung asks how King would adapt her oversight approach to New York City jails. King says the state prison and city jail oversight roles are parallel and that New York City needs fundamental reform in management, staffing, training, and information systems to change jail culture.
chapters.title: Chair Ung asks King how she would adapt oversight to NYC jails

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: How will you adapt the oversight approaches you use in Canny to the unique challenges of the New York City jail system?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I mean, I think they're very parallel, and I think the experience chairing the Correctional Association's board and the experience of what we've seen

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: in the New York State prison system directly relate to what we need in the New York City jails, which I believe is fundamental reform.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I think we've been...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Trying to fix some of the, around the edges of the problems when I think we really need fundamental management and staffing and training and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: information systems change that would ultimately reform the culture of the organization.

chapters.summary: Minority Leader Carr asks whether the Department of Correction should continue refusing ICE detainer requests. King says DOC should follow city law and that she would not advocate changing local law to allow cooperation, opposing cooperation before conviction.
chapters.title: Minority Leader Carr questions King on ICE detainer cooperation

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: We've been joined by Deputy Speaker Williams, and now I'm going to pass it off to Minority Leader Carr.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you for being here today.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I want to talk to you a little bit about, I guess, what's commonly called our sanctuary city policies.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Do you believe that the Department of Correction should continue to refuse to cooperate with ICE detainer requests?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I believe that the department should follow the laws that are set out by the city council and the mayor.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So if the law was, would you advocate a change in local law in order to allow the Department of Correction to cooperate with ICE?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I would not.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Could you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I don't believe that cooperation prior to someone's conviction of a crime furthers public safety or justice.

chapters.summary: Carr asks whether King would support cooperating with ICE for people with prior convictions. King says felony convictions require communication with the federal government but that she does not think people should be handed over to ICE, adding that she is not a lawyer.
chapters.title: Carr questions King on prior convictions and ICE handovers

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So if someone was incarcerated at Rikers and had prior convictions, you would support cooperating with ICE in those conditions?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: If they were convicted of a felony, I believe that they are required to communicate with the federal government about that.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: But not for a misdemeanor offense?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I must say I'm not a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Oh, I'm asking you your opinion.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about what's legally required.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Do you believe that someone has prior convictions and notwithstanding local law that they should be handed over to ICE if there's a detainer request issued by that federal agency?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: No, I don't think they should be handed over.

chapters.summary: Carr argues that local law blocks administrative ICE detainers and asks whether that is good public safety policy. King says the city is following the law and she does not see it as non-cooperation. Carr calls it definitional non-cooperation and ends his questioning.
chapters.title: Carr challenges King on public safety and non-cooperation with ICE

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I think that's sort of a difficult position to maintain, right?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: We have people who have been incarcerated previously.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: They've been convicted of crimes.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: These are people who already violated our immigration laws one way or the other, either by entry or by remaining or both.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: What public safety interest is really served by allowing these individuals to remain in the United States and to not cooperate with federal immigration law enforcement?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I think that we have good laws currently about people who pose public safety risks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: After they've been released, after they've been convicted, after they've been released, there is communication between local, state, and federal authorities to follow our current immigration laws.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: But there's currently a local law that the Department of Correction is following, right, that's being litigated in court right now that precludes anything other than a judicial warrant from being acted upon by the department.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Now, most ICE detainer requests, in fact, virtually all ICE detainer requests are administratively issued.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So we have a federal law enforcement agency that's trying to do its job, and we have a municipal agency that's refusing to cooperate with it.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: You think that's good public safety policy?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I don't see it that way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I don't see it as non-cooperation and not following the law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I think the city is following the law.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I think when an agency issues a request or an order and it's not cooperating,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I thought you said they needed a judicial order.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: No, well, that's what the local law says, right?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: But I'm asking you substantively why you think that it's not non-cooperation when it's a field detainer request.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I mean, it's the very definition of non-cooperation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I don't know what to say about that, sir.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I don't know what to say about that either.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Riley asks about DOC organizational and cultural problems and the Board's role. King supports borough-based jails but says they are not a magic bullet, citing dysfunctional staff supervision, recruitment and training problems, paper-based systems, and management not knowing staff deployment.
chapters.title: Councilmember Riley questions King on borough-based jails and DOC culture

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Now I'd like to pass it off to Councilmember Raleigh, and we've also been joined by Councilmember Banks.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: King.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: How are you doing today?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I just wanted to focus my questions on the borough-based jails and appreciate you taking your time to testify in front of us today.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: In your response to the pre-hearing questions, you noted that longstanding organizational and cultural problems with the DOC.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Can you please expand on those problems and explain what role are you feel the board can play in alleviating the new jail system?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So I believe strongly that the borough-based jails and bringing people who are detained pre-trial closer to their families and friends and to the courts is absolutely essential.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I don't think it's a magic bullet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: It won't solve all of the problems in the jails.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I think the board's role is not only to monitor the development and transition into the new jails, but really it is to focus on whether or not those new jails deliver on the promise of more safety

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: and better conditions for staff and people who are in custody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: To your question about what kinds of changes we know we need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I think based upon the Board of Corrections reports, on the reports from the Federal Monitor, we know that there are significantly dysfunctional supervision and support

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: systems for staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: We have a recruitment problem and we have a training problem for staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: We also have information systems based on paper that are very illegible and hard to translate into knowing what's going on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So one of the major findings of the federal court has been that the management of the Department of Correction doesn't actually know where their staff is deployed at any given time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So solving that problem could be huge for solving many other problems.

chapters.summary: Riley asks how the Board and DOC should respond if the jail population is not reduced in time for borough-based jails. King says delays and costs are concerning, about 2,200 people above planned capacity, and urges planning now, faster court case processing, and alternatives for seriously mentally ill people.
chapters.title: Riley asks King about contingency if jail population is not reduced

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: King.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And assuming the relevant stakeholders are unable to sufficiently draw down the jail population in time from the transition to the borough-based jail system, how would you propose the board and the DOC respond to that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: It's a huge concern.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: We're obviously delayed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: The costs are escalating, and it's like 2,200 people above the capacity currently of the planned borough jails.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I think we should start planning now, and we need to have a bunch of contingency plans for whether or not we can meet that goal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I believe that the city needs to work very closely with the court system on speeding up case processing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: We have many people, 500 people there for more than two years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: There are people languishing there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I mean, the court shouldn't.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: move faster, that would significantly reduce the number of people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: We have 20% of the people in jail who are seriously mentally ill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: That's unprecedented.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And the numbers have just been going up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And so we need a focused plan to, with the courts, to have other options for people with serious mental illness who are not being served well by being in a jail.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: That's where I would focus.

chapters.summary: Riley asks about risks from delays and escalating costs and what role the Board can play. King says BOC's unfettered access and sole focus on city jails let it identify problems early and bring data to the Council, while warning against assuming borough jails will fail and stressing the need for a Plan B.
chapters.title: Riley asks King about borough jail risks and BOC reporting role

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: King.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I guess one more question before I pass it back to the chair.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: In your pre-hearing question and response, you noted that continuing delays and escalating costs are creating the risk to borrow brace jails projects itself, in which you just mentioned your answer.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Can you please expand on those risks and what role, if any, the board can play in either managing them directly or reporting them for the benefit of policymakers to make the right decisions with policies?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So I think the board, because of its unfettered access and because of its sole focus on the New York City jails, they have the ability to bring,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: to identify problems earlier than many other stakeholders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And they can do that by talking with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: The management and with staff and with people who are in custody and bringing to light and to the council as much data as possible that the jails have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I think

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: You know, we have a risk of planning too much that as if the borough based jails won't happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So we don't want to fall into a place where we, you know, make that fulfill that prophecy ourselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: But I think we also need to be cognizant that we need plan B also.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Totally understood.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: King.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Deputy Speaker Williams notes 15 deaths in DOC custody in 2025 and seven so far this year. King says BOC must investigate each death and should also look across deaths for recurrent failures, lack of prevention, and lack of urgency.
chapters.title: Deputy Speaker Williams questions King on deaths in custody

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And now I'm going to pass it off to our deputy speaker.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Hi.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Hi.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Just a few questions on death in custody.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: 15 people died in DOC custody in 2025, and seven have died so far this year.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: If confirmed, how would you approach reviewing those deaths, and what changes would you advocate to improve safety in jails?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: As you know, the Board of Correction is required to investigate each of those deaths, and I think the Board has been issuing very important and illuminating reports about each of those deaths.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I think additionally what the Board

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I hope the board would do if I were appointed would be to look back on a regular basis, not just at one death, but at the patterns we see across all of those deaths, because we see recurrent

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: failures and we see recurrent actions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: That make people unsafe and a lack of prevention and a lack of urgency in addressing deaths.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And I think while it's very important to look at each individual death,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: We have to look across the deaths and highlight those patterns for the management and for the council and for the public.

chapters.summary: Williams asks how to make information about deaths in DOC custody more timely and accessible. King says BOC reports are currently the most timely and transparent but that a retrospective, comprehensive accounting of deaths is needed alongside individual investigations.
chapters.title: Williams asks King about transparency on deaths in custody

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: At the Correctional Association, you helped improve transparency around prison deaths.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: What steps would you take to make information about deaths in DOC custody more timely and accessible to the public?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So, you know, the board's reports currently are the most timely and transparent, I think, of the different death investigations that are out there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: What we don't always have is like a retrospective, comprehensive accounting of the number of deaths and who is dying and why.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And we need that alongside investigation, sort of like the basic data and landscape, and then in addition to the investigations, which is what the Correctional Association is issuing as well.

chapters.summary: Williams congratulates King on recently completing her doctorate and asks how her dissertation research on 159 deaths shaped her view. King says problems are consistent across jail settings, death rates were higher outside New York City in her study, and the Board should take a systemic look at care and accountability failures.
chapters.title: Williams asks King about her dissertation research on jail deaths

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: In your dissertation research, which I guess we should be calling you Dr.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: King.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I just passed last week.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Oh, yay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Oh, congratulations.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So wait, so you graduate?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Whenever they walk, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: CUNY.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Oh, CUNY grad from John Jay?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Most of my committee was from John Javits through the Graduate Center.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, me too.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I'm a CUNY grad too.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Silberman.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Well, your dissertation research examined 100 and...

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: 59 deaths in New York County and New York City jails over a five-year period.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You identify recurring patterns preceding many deaths, including inadequate screenings, insufficient supervision, medical and mental health care, substance use treatment, communication, and record keeping.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: How have those findings shaped your view on the board's role in investigating deaths in custody?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And what changes, if any, would you advocate for the board's approach to investigating deaths in custody?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And so it has, I think it would bring my experience from that research, looking at all of the county jails in New York, and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: as much attention as we put in Rikers Island, and as we should, I will say that the problems are pretty consistent across different jail settings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And that's actually the period I was looking at the rate of deaths was higher outside of New York City than here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: That being said, I think, you know, part of what I learned from that research, again, was really not just looking at

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: one death, but looking across deaths so that one can take a systemic look

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: at what is failing in terms of the delivery of services, the delivery of care, what is failing in terms of accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: That's a large problem with the deaths is that staff, for instance,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: who are not following the policies of supervision or not following the policies of screening, which is so important when people come in to identify any dangers or concerns, that those people need to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: That issue needs to be...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Pointed out by management and those people need either to be counseled or disciplined or retrained.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And it's not just that person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: It's really all of the staff need to learn from each of those individual deaths and the patterns we see across them.

chapters.summary: Williams asks for comparative county death rates. King says Monroe, Suffolk, Nassau, and Erie counties had higher death rates than New York City and that smaller jails often have higher rates, but her pre-COVID research is dated and she will send updated numbers.
chapters.title: Williams follows up on comparative county death rates

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You said New York City, in comparison, the deaths are significantly, would you say significantly lower?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Like what are the averages versus like New York?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I would just love like comparatively what you see in the other counties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So death rates are subject to a lot of change year to year in a jail.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: It's Monroe, Suffolk, Nassau, and Erie counties are the ones that had higher death rates than New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And also, and this follows national patterns, that smaller jails tend to have higher rates of death than much larger jails.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: It could be related to the resources we have, more resources we have in health care and mental health care and larger systems.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So, like, we've had 15 deaths.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Like, do you know, like, how many, like, they've had in a year versus, like, I just, I'm very interested in the

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: The number.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: One of the problems with dissertation research is that it's a little dated now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: But I would happily send you updated numbers.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: It was pre-COVID, my research, because COVID altered the patterns of death so drastically in jails.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Banks asks how serving as a Board member differs from serving as Executive Director. King says Board members are public-facing, lead hearings, vote on regulations and resolutions, coordinate with DOC management, and set priorities for staff to implement.
chapters.title: Councilmember Banks asks King about board member vs executive director role

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And we've been joined by Councilmember Lee and Felder.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And now I'd like to pass it off to Councilmember Banks.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I see that you, as the executive actor, also versus a board member, your resume shows you led the Board of Corrections as the executive director from 2015 to 2019.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How is serving as a board member different, and what will you do differently in this role?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: The board members versus the staff and the executive director are very different roles, and I'm much more cognizant of those differences having served as executive director previously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: The board members really serve a public-facing role, so leading public hearings, following the evidence produced by staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: voting on regulations and resolutions publicly, coordinating at high levels with the management of the department, and really the board members work together to set priorities

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: and set an agenda that then staff implement.

chapters.summary: Banks asks whether solitary confinement should be banned and what role BOC should play in implementing Local Law 42. King supports keeping the ban, cites serious harm and lack of deterrence evidence, and says DOC needs comprehensive violence prevention, incentives, and behavior management.
chapters.title: Banks questions King on Local Law 42 and solitary confinement

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Let me go into the local law 42.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I was actually proud to be a part of the council that passed local law 42 to restrict solitary confinement and strengthen protections for incarcerated people.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Do you believe solitary confinement should be banned in city jails, and what role should the BOC play in implementing this law?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I do believe that solitary should be prohibited and the ban should remain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I think there's extensive evidence that shows the serious physical and psychological harm caused by solitary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And at the same time, we don't have evidence that solitary deterred violence or made the jail safer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: At the same time, it's not a sufficient condition to create safety in the jails.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I think it's necessary, but not sufficient.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: The Department of Correction really needs a comprehensive and focused approach to violence prevention and responses to violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And that goes well beyond.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: It should have always gone beyond solitary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: It's about incentives and behavior management.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: and following the data about why violence is occurring.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: The board's role, you know, when I was executive director, there were early reforms to solitary in terms of preventing young people from going in and people with serious mental illness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And the board's consistent release of data and of monitoring how those changes were implemented, I think, helped further the reductions that we saw then.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And I think the board's monitoring can help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Further the better implementation of that local law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I know within the confines of the federal courts position.

chapters.summary: Banks asks what alternatives DOC should pursue to reduce violence while maintaining safety. King says the focus must be on prevention, programming, reliable recreation, de-escalation, and separation of people who commit violence, noting solitary did not ensure those responses.
chapters.title: Banks asks King about alternatives to reduce violence

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What specific alternatives should DOC pursue to reduce violence while maintaining safety for both the staff and people in custody?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So I think the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: We get caught in a very bad cycle that's not productive of thinking about only responses to violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: It's very important that we think before violence happens and all of the work that needs to be done to prevent violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: That being said, which is about programming and keeping people occupied, it's about reliably delivering on our obligations as a city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: If we say you have access to recreation, you should get recreation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So all of that has to happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: But then responding to violence, the actual separation of people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: people who have committed acts of violence is critical.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: The de-escalation among anyone involved in violence is critical.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And the existence of solitary didn't mean that that actually happened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So I think the focus needs to be on immediate de-escalation and separation of people who have committed violence.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how the Board should monitor whether people in custody receive due process protections under Local Law 42. King says BOC can access all jail areas, including hearing rooms, and should observe due process hearings to illuminate compliance for DOC, the Council, and New Yorkers.
chapters.title: Banks asks how BOC should monitor due process under Local Law 42

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And how should the board monitor whether

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: people in custody are receiving due process protections required under local law of 42.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: That's a good question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: You know, one of the privileges of the Board of Correction is to go to and access any part of the jail, including hearing rooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And the board has observed hearings in the past, and I think there could be a very important focused look at all of the due process hearings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: That would be very illuminating for the Department of Correction and for New Yorkers and the council.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Lee notes Rikers is now the third-largest mental health institution in the country and asks what is working and what needs improvement. King says serious mental illness has risen to 20 percent, state hospital beds and treatment courts are needed, jail worsens mental illness, and intensive health-staffed units help.
chapters.title: Councilmember Lee questions King on mental health and Rikers
