utterances.text: Q, and now I will pass it all to Councilmember Lee.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Hi, good morning.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And apologies if you went through this.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I was a little late.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: But as a social worker myself, former chair of the mental health committee, you know, we went, one of the things I did in my earlier years on the council was working on the mental health roadmap.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And one of the things we focused on was the

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: the pillar was the intersectionality between criminal justice and mental health, which is a big thing.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And I've learned a lot about, you know, went on a visit, saw the facilities at Rikers, you know, after health and hospitals took over, and just really wanted to hear your honest feedback in terms of

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: From your perspective, what are things that are working well?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: What are things we need to improve on?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Because Rikers is now the third largest mental health institution in the country.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so how can we better utilize?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: treatment courts, what's needed with staffing, if you could just give us a little bit more of the landscape and what you think could be worked on and improved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: We touched on it only a second before you were here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So, you know, I think the numbers of people who are seriously mentally ill have continued to rise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: It's quite shocking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I think from where we were when I was executive director 10 years ago to where we are today with 20% of people having a serious mental illness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So I think we need like all hands on deck from the state and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: state investment in hospital beds and psychiatric inpatient and outpatient treatment, as well as the court systems involvement, as you said, in expanding treatment court options.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: We need the judges and the court system to think about the variety of custodial options for people with mental illness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Jail can only worsen someone's mental illness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: It doesn't get people better.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And obviously we have a revolving door between the state and the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I will say to the credit of the city health system running the health care in the jails, there are some very small innovations that do

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: reduce harm, such as you probably saw intensive units that are much more highly staffed by health care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: staff or people with serious mental illness, those are very important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Could those be in a hospital?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Perhaps.

chapters.summary: Lee follows up on referrals and handoffs for people with severe mental illness. King says court and judicial involvement determine disposition and that she is not best positioned to detail the process, but agrees the Council should stay updated.
chapters.title: Lee follows up on referrals and handoffs for severe mental illness

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And as you alluded to, though, the number of beds is a real issue.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And I know that on the council, we really tried hard to expand the types of beds available for folks with severe mental illness.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: But in terms of the referrals, if you deem someone who has severe mental illness, what does that look like then in terms of the referral and the handoff for them to receive treatment versus being in the jail system?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So that's a good question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm best positioned to answer it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I mean, if the court's involved, right, we would need the judge's involvement in making that disposition about where that person would be held.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Yeah, yes.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And I know it's not obviously something we're going to solve here in this moment, but just to let us know and keep us updated in terms of where as a council we can help, because I know there's several members that are very invested in this issue.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So if we can push both.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: There's several pieces, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Before they get to the point where they land in Rikers, and then also after that point, what does the care look like and what does that system look like in terms of how we can uplift those folks?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So anyway, I just wanted to put that out there.

chapters.summary: King adds that supportive housing is the most cost-effective way to keep people out of jail and that about 50 percent of seriously mentally ill people are homeless. Lee says JISH funding was increased but still feels insufficient.
chapters.title: King adds supportive housing point; Lee notes JISH funding gap

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I would be remiss if I didn't mention supportive housing and that we know that that's the most cost-effective way to keep people out of jail.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And I think it's like 50% of...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: of the seriously mentally ill people are homeless.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Yes, and we did put more funding in for JISH, but I feel like it's not enough.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Felder says regular jail often feels like solitary confinement and asks about King's proposal. King agrees conditions outside punitive segregation must change with programming, visits, outside access, and a reliable comprehensive disciplinary system with incentives and sanctions.
chapters.title: Councilmember Felder questions King on solitary and jail conditions

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I'd like now to pass it off to Council Member Felder.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: I just want to follow up on Councilman Banks'discussion about solitary.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: So when I was in the Senate, I visited a number of jails in New York State.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: I mean, forget about solitary confinement.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: A regular jail is solitary confinement.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: And it's solitary.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: So I understood what you said, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: I don't know if there is an answer, but I'm not sure I understood

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: what your proposal was to the actual solitary confinement that they have today in jails.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to pick up on two points you made.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I think you were suggesting that much of what jail looks like looks like solitary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So that must be changed, and that means that when people are in

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: not punished or under some kind of punitive sanction, it shouldn't look the same.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: There should be programming and access to visits and outside and ways to keep people occupied and to move through the court process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So that should look very different.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And I think that's one of the problems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: You know, that we can't just focus on solitary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: We have to focus on the conditions outside of it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And I think what I was trying to say about reform and keeping the prohibition on solitary is that it's very important that we respond to violence seriously and make sure that people are kept separate and that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: situations are de-escalated, but then also that there are, it's a comprehensive disciplinary system that involves incentives and sanctions and is reliable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: It has to be, you know, they have to implement it for all people all the time, and that has not been the case historically.

chapters.summary: Chair Ung asks how well the Department of Correction complies with BOC standards. King says policies exist but implementation is inconsistent and DOC lacks information systems to track recreation, programs, and staff deployment, so better data is needed to monitor compliance.
chapters.title: Chair Ung questions King on DOC compliance with BOC standards

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Bless you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And I just have a few more questions about oversight compliance.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: How well do you think the Department of Corrections is in complying with the BOC standards?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So the board standards are extensive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And I think, you know, clearly the department has the rules, the policies in place that are reflective of the board standards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: There becomes an issue in implementation and the consistent following of those standards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: The bigger problem, I believe, is that the department lacks information systems to actually know when, for instance, how many people are going to recreation and when.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: It lacks the systems to know when people are going to programs or not, and it lacks the ability to actually know where their staff is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So I think...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is there are certainly problems with compliance with the standards, but we first and foremost need better information to accurately monitor compliance with the standards.

chapters.summary: Chair Ung notes outdated record keeping and asks what improvements are needed in communication between DOC and the Board. King says BOC has restored unfettered access after prior obstruction and that communication is best when management, staff, and systems communicate.
chapters.title: Chair Ung asks about record-keeping and DOC-BOC communication

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: We've also been joined by Councilman Krishna.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: In your pre-hearing question responses, you noted that the outdated record keeping makes compliance difficult to track.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: What improvements are needed to improve communication between DLC and the board?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Good question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So right now, I think the board has restored unfettered access to the department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: That hasn't always been the case under the last administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I think there were a variety of ways that the board was obstructed by the administration, by the Department of Correction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I think the communication, as long as management and staff and the systems are communicating, that's the best that we could hope for.

chapters.summary: Chair Ung asks what additional tools the Board should have to hold DOC accountable when violations persist. King says BOC already has tools that are not consistently used, including audits, public reporting, resolutions, corrective action plans, and notices of public violation.
chapters.title: Chair Ung asks what additional tools BOC needs for accountability

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: In your pre-hearing question responses, you said that compliance can look stronger on paper than in practice.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: What additional tools, if any, should the board have to hold the OLC accountable when violations persist?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So right now, I think the board does have a variety of tools that are not always used or not consistently used.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And that starts with audits and starts with public reporting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: It moves on to resolutions and corrective action plans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And then it moves on to notices of public violation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: At that point, it is up to the court of public opinion and our elected officials to back the Board of Corrections'findings of issues within the jails.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Krishnan asks how BOC oversight can address staffing and operational failures identified in the 2025 Nunez report. King says BOC identifies causes with stakeholders, audits over time, develops solutions, and must consistently use escalating responses to noncompliance.
chapters.title: Councilmember Krishnan questions King on Nunez report and BOC oversight

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Now I'd like to pass it off to Councilman Vikrishnan.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Sher.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Good morning, Martha.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Good to see you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Good to see you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I just had a few questions building on some of the themes that have already been addressed.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And one is, as you know, the 2025 Nunez report has pointed to persistent staffing and operational failures at Rikers.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: How can BOC's oversight help to address those problems and ensure that all the recommendations are put in place to improve conditions and overall oversight at our jail?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So I think the board's value lies within its ability to identify the cause of a problem in speaking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: with all the different stakeholders that are impacted by a problem, and then

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: developing the information to accurately audit over time how that problem is manifesting in the jails, and then developing solutions based upon

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: practices from outside of New York City, but also with conversation of management about how to address those.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: As I was just mentioning, I think the Board of Correction has a toolkit of escalating responses to noncompliance that it needs to use consistently,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: which I think will further the department's implementation of its policies.

chapters.summary: Krishnan says the new administration shares his values, wants Rikers closed as quickly as possible, and wants federal litigation and consent decrees implemented. He appreciates King's approach to the Board's critical role.
chapters.title: Krishnan comments on new administration and closing Rikers

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I appreciate that and appreciate your perspective also in how to implement the findings and recommendations from the Nunez report too.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I think now we have a real opportunity with the new administration that shares finally the same values that I certainly do and many others of.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Ultimately closing down Rikers Island and as quick as possible and ensuring that the federal litigation and the consent decrees are actually implemented.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So I know that you all have a critical role in doing so and appreciate your approach to it.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks what accountability measures DOC should use to ensure supervisors enforce protocols. King says Rikers is known for failed staff accountability, investigations drag on unresolved, and staff must be held accountable for management to direct them; this is central to the Nunez consent decree.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks about accountability for supervisors enforcing protocols

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: My other question is when basic security failures continue despite years of oversight, what accountability measures should DOC use to ensure supervisors are enforcing established protocols?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So we have a, Rikers, I guess, is known probably for the failed accountability and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: discipline of its staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: We know that investigations into staff misconduct have dragged on and never been resolved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Like you said, I think we have a moment of opportunity to really address that problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: But until

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: staff are held accountable and told what cannot be done, management can't tell what staff to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So in other words, you have to be able to say, no, this cannot be done if you're going to actually tell staff what can be done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So I think the, I'm sure the administration is focused on improving accountability for staff, and I think that should be a priority.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: It's at the center of the Nunez consent decree, and I think it's also something that the board should continue to look at.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks how the Board can determine whether DOC addresses underlying causes of staffing and supervision failures rather than individual incidents. King cites a proposed early intervention system for staff and Board audits using video to compare staff records with reality.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks how BOC can assess systemic causes vs individual incidents

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And relatedly, how could the board determine whether DOC is addressing the underlying causes of staffing and supervision failures rather than simply responding to individual incidents?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: How can the board determine or look more closely into whether DOC is addressing the underlying causes of staffing and supervision failures rather than simply responding to individual incidents?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So in other words, as you just pointed out as well, we need to get beyond these individual issues and failures and understand the larger systemic reasons behind them.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: How do you see BOC's role in ensuring that DOC is able to do so?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Well, there's probably...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Probably a couple of ways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: One, the department some years ago discussed the development of an early intervention system for staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: In other words, if you see staff, you know, with not doing sort of the smaller things, how do you counsel and supervise and support that staff to really learn the job and follow the rules and regulations?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So that has fallen away, I believe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I think the board could...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Push that idea further.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: The board's audits of using video to actually follow whether or not

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: staff's records are reflective of reality is another way that the board helps the department and the public understand where staff are meeting their obligations and where they are falling short.

chapters.summary: Krishnan describes a DOI report on improper information sharing and asks how BOC ensures sanctuary laws are followed at individual and systemic levels. King says BOC can attend and assess trainings, talk with staff about their knowledge, and audit individual paperwork to see changes since the DOI report.
chapters.title: Krishnan questions King on sanctuary laws and DOI report

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And my final question that kind of combines those two together and applies it to an ongoing situation we have was we have our sanctuary laws in New York City, as you well know.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Earlier this year, my committee, the Oversight Committee, we had done a hearing about ensuring that the sanctuary laws were being enforced and implemented in reality.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: As I always say, our laws are not worth more than the paper they're written on if they're not actually enforced and followed in reality.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And DOI put out a very critical report about the last administration and the way in which information was being impermissibly shared.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: within corrections at Rikers, also then YPD, and issued a series of recommendations to ensure that, in this instance, DOC

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: is adhering to our sanctuary law policies and ensure that there are no violations of them, whether intentional or not.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We had a very productive hearing earlier in the year.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: DOC leadership confirmed under this administration, as opposed to the last one, their real commitment to making sure that DOI's findings and recommendations are implemented

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: and that the sanctuary laws are taken much more seriously by this administration than the last one.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And as a follow-up to that, my question is, given that...

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: There can be individual failures that result in violations of our sanctuary laws in such a crucial moment when there's so much fear and presence of ICE across our communities and neighborhoods like mine.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: There are individual instances, but they can also reveal larger systemic problems.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so one of the things that we had talked about at the hearing was DOC instituting trainings in place to make sure that employees at Rikers Island know what the sanctuary laws are, know what is impermissible cooperation with ICE and city and federal government.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And that's really important.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I think also there are other measures, too, that can be taken to really protect our sanctuary laws in this moment because ICE does not care about them.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I've seen those instances over and over again in my own district, and we've all seen it across the city.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So my question is, with BOC in particular, how do we ensure that from an individual level,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: and a systemic level that the Department of Corrections is both implementing DOI's protocols and doing all that it can do to ensure our sanctuary laws are carefully followed in every instance in Rikers Island.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I think that's a great example of how, you know, if the board identifies a priority and when

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: we as a city have identified a problem as with the DOI report that the board can effectuate really unique ongoing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: investigations and audits of how the law is being followed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: You know, board can attend trainings for the Department of Correction staff and make assessments about whether or not that training is

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: in compliance with the law and as effective as it should be for staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: It can talk to staff about whether or not they know the law and how to follow policy in their jobs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: We also could look at

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: the paperwork for each individual, like take an audit of a series of individuals and look at whether or not anything has changed since the Department of Investigation report.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Lee follows up on record-keeping and interagency systems, asking what systems DOC and BOC use and how they communicate with partner agencies. King says systems are outdated and make it difficult to track patterns, and BOC should examine communication points from police to DOC, health services, and community providers.
chapters.title: Lee follows up on record-keeping and interagency systems

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I believe Council Member Lee has a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Sorry, hi.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask, go on a little bit of a deeper dive to a follow-up on Chair Ung's question around the oversight and compliance and the outdated record-keeping, because just out of curiosity,

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Because one of the things that I used to get frustrated with on the social service provider side when I was on that end of it was the different silos in government and how the systems don't necessarily talk to each other, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And just wondering from your perspective, what systems are you currently using just for record keeping as well as communicating internally with DOC?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: How do those systems then communicate out to other agencies that you partner with a lot and that you communicate with a lot?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And then how could that also help with oversight, of course, while keeping privacy?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And I'll just give one small example is that a lot of the times what we hear on the ground in a totally different setting with the housing folks as well as the food providers is that if they could just

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: simply put the housing questionnaire and the food SNAP benefit questionnaire on the same application, it would tremendously help with streamlining.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So are there things like that that you see within DOC, BOC that would be helpful in the staff doing the day-to-day and helping them to do the work that they're doing?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: So since I haven't been at the board for a little bit of time, I'm not totally sure of their current access or up to date on their systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: From my past experience, what I know from the outside, the department and the board have had very outdated systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: Digital system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And it makes it very difficult to understand what's happening or to track patterns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I think you're raising a really important idea, which is actually having the board look at all of those points where there are opportunities for better communication.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: I can think about from the police department to the Department of Correction, for instance, at the beginning, or between health services and correction while people are in custody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Martha King
utterances.text: And then, of course, when people are returning to the community, there should be better communication and shared systems for community providers as well as the people who are running the jail or the health care.

chapters.summary: Lee says the systems likely have not changed much since King left and asks her to keep the Council updated. Lee notes that poor systems also prevent district attorneys' offices from being more efficient with cases and moving people through the system faster.
chapters.title: Lee urges King to keep Council updated on systems and DA efficiency

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So if you're in that position to take a look at that, that'd be great.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: It probably hasn't changed much since you left, I would guess.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee

chapters.summary: Chair Ung reviews the City Planning Commission's responsibilities, including planning for city growth, reviewing zoning map and text changes, ULURP, environmental review, capital strategy, and rules for land use actions.
chapters.title: Chair Ung reviews City Planning Commission functions

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Before I introduce the candidates, I will review the functions and membership qualifications of CPC.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The City Planning Commission is responsible for the conduct of planning relating to the already growth, improvement, and future development of the city.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: of the city, including adequate and appropriate resources for the housing, business, industry, transportation, distribution, recreation, culture, comfort, convenience, health, and the welfare of its population.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The CPC is also responsible for the review of and has a veto power over all proposals to change the zoning map, the city map, and the text of the zoning resolution.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Site selections for city capital projects or major concessions, proposed franchises, revocable consents that the Department of City Planning determines would have land use impact.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Proposed housing and urban renewal plans pursuant to state and federal law, sales, acquisitions, leases, and other dispositions of real property often by the city, and the granting of special permits pursuant to the zoning resolution.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The CPC oversees the implementation of laws that require environmental reviews of actions taken by the city, in particular the City Environmental Quality Review, the State Environmental Quality Review Act, and the National Environmental Policy Act.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The CPC assists the mayor and other officials in developing the 10-year capital strategy, the four-year capital program, as well as the annual statement of needs.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The CPC is also responsible for promulgating various rules, including establishing the minimal standards for certification of applications that are subject to the Uniform Land Use Review Procedure.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Establishing the minimal standards and procedural requirements for the community boards, borough presidents, borough boards, the commission itself in the exercise of the

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: duties and their responsibilities in your life.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Establishing specific time periods for pre-certification review of applications subject to Europe.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Establishing the procedure for environmental reviews required by law, including the procedures for the preparation and filing of environmental assessment statements and environmental impact studies.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Establishing the minimum standards and the form and content of 197A plans.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And listing major concessions or establishing a procedure for determining whether a concession is defined as a major concession.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The CPC also the power to modify any amendments proposed by the mayor to change the rules governing the site selection and the fair distribution of all city facilities.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The commission also has exclusive power to propose additional categories of land use action to be reviewed pursuant to ULIP, subject to the enactment by the council.

chapters.summary: Chair Ung explains that the CPC has 13 members chosen for independence, integrity, and civic commitment. Members other than the chair are not regular city employees, cannot hold other city office, and have no term limits.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: There are no limitations on the numbers a term a CBC member may serve.

chapters.summary: Anthony Crowell thanks the Chair, Deputy Speaker, and members, and says after four years on the CPC he wants to continue serving. He describes a career dedicated to public service, affordability, equity, sustainability, and responsible growth.
chapters.title: Anthony Crowell opening statement: public service and housing goals

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I'm happy to go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Chair and Deputy Speaker and members of the committee for this opportunity to appear before you today to discuss my nomination for reappointment to the City Planning Commission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I'm Anthony Crowell.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I want to thank those council members also who met with me during the pre-hearing process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And who took the time to share their questions, perspectives, and concerns regarding the future of land use planning in our city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: After four years of service on the commission, my desire to continue serving remains strong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: My entire career as a lawyer and organizational leader has been dedicated to public service, building institutions, communities, and systems that better serve human needs and advance justice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Whether in local government, higher education, community development, or civic leadership, I have always believed that effective public service begins with listening, collaboration, and a commitment to improving people's lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I care deeply about making New York City affordable and accessible to those who need homes and jobs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I care deeply about making our city more equitable, sustainable, safe, healthy, and economically vibrant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And I believe that...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Thoughtful planning and responsible growth are essential to achieving those goals.

chapters.summary: Crowell says New York faces an extraordinary affordable housing shortage requiring cooperation across government. He says he has approached CPC work with independence, objectivity, and respect for facts, weighing both benefits and burdens of proposed actions.
chapters.title: Crowell on housing challenges and commission principles

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Today, New York faces extraordinary challenges, particularly the continuing shortage of affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Addressing that challenge requires cooperation across every level of government and a recognition that both citywide and neighborhood needs matter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: We must continue to identify opportunities to expand housing, support businesses, strengthen infrastructure, reduce environmental impacts, and improve quality of life for current and future New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Over the last four years, I have approached my work on the Commission with independence, objectivity, and respect for the facts before the Commission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I have sought to understand both the benefits and burdens of proposed actions, recognizing that our decisions affect both individual neighborhoods and also the broader future of our city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Those principles would continue to guide my service if I am reappointed.

chapters.summary: Crowell commits to implementing the 2025 charter revisions while ensuring the CPC remains attentive to Council members, community boards, and residents. He values robust communication with the Council and wants an efficient, inclusive planning process.
chapters.title: Crowell on 2025 charter revisions and Council/community role

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: As this committee knows, the city's land use framework has recently undergone significant change following the 2025 charter revisions approved by the voters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: As a commissioner, I am committed to faithfully carrying out those responsibilities while ensuring that the commission remains highly attentive to the voices of council members, as well as community boards and the residents they represent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Throughout my nearly 30 years of service to New York City, I have always greatly respected and valued the role of the Council and viewed the relationship between the Council and the Commission as an essential one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I continue to believe that robust communication and collaboration with council members strengthens land use decision making.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: The recent changes make that commitment even more important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: While certain formal roles in the process have evolved, the need to hear and understand local concerns has not diminished.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I have expressed my view that the Commission should continue to benefit from clear and meaningful input from elected officials,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: community boards, and community members, and I will continue working with Commission leadership to ensure that those perspectives inform our deliberations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: New Yorkers deserve a planning process that is both efficient and inclusive, one that advances urgently needed housing and economic opportunity while respecting democratic participation and community engagement.

chapters.summary: Crowell describes his working-class family, being first in his family to attend college, attending law school at night, and his mother's family coming to Brooklyn. He worked in city government since 1997, in Bloomberg City Hall, and now leads New York Law School.
chapters.title: Crowell describes personal background and career

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: My perspective on these issues is shaped by both my professional and personal experiences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I come from a working class family and was the first in my family to attend college, and I attended law school at night while working full time during the day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: My mother's family came to Brooklyn in the early 20th century seeking refuge and opportunity, and like countless other New Yorkers, they relied on the promise that this city could create a better future for the next generation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: That belief continues to guide me today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I studied urban policy and planning as an undergraduate because I wanted to help make cities more just and effective.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I worked on housing, land use, environmental, and community development issues before and during my service to the city, which started in 1997 when I was an entry-level lawyer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: at the City Law Department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Following that service for more than a decade, I worked in City Hall in the Bloomberg administration on a broad range of matters affecting neighborhoods throughout the city, including 9-11 recovery, economic development and small businesses, land use and government reform.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Those experiences reinforced my belief that planning and implementation are inseparable and that good policy succeeds only when government remains accountable to the people it serves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Today, as Dean and President of New York Law School, I continue to work closely with students whose lives reflect the diversity, aspirations, and challenges of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Many are first-generation college and professional students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Many work while attending school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Many struggle with housing affordability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Their experiences remind me every day that land use decisions have real-life on-the-ground impacts and are not simply policy abstractions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: They shape whether people can afford to live, work, and build their futures in our city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: That is why during my tenure at New York Law School, we have built one of the strongest public interest housing law and policy programs among the nation's law schools.

chapters.summary: Crowell closes by citing integrity, transparency, accountability, and independence as pillars of democratic good government. He commits to listening and collaborating with fellow commissioners, the Council, the administration, community boards, and New Yorkers.
chapters.title: Crowell closes with principles of good government

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Throughout my career, whether in government, leading academic institutions, or serving on public boards, I have relied on four principles that I often describe as the pillars of democratic good government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Integrity, transparency, accountability, and independence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Those principles have guided my service on the commission and would continue to guide me if confirmed for another term.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I remain committed to listening, learning, and working collaboratively with my fellow commissioners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: council, the administration, community boards, civic stakeholders, and New Yorkers from every neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Our city's future depends on our ability to find common ground and build solutions that serve both today's needs and tomorrow's generations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Thank you for your consideration.

chapters.summary: Meenakshi Srinivasan thanks the Chair, Deputy Speaker, and members and says she is honored to be considered. She describes 36 years as an urban planner in New York and senior roles in public and private sectors, including leadership at three city land use agencies.
chapters.title: Meenakshi Srinivasan opening statement: career overview

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Ang, Deputy Speaker Williams, and members of the Committee on Rules, Privileges, Election Standards, and Ethics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: It is an honor to be considered for an appointment to the City Planning Commission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Mayor Mamdani, Deputy Mayor Bozorg, and Chair Sherman for their support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I welcome the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: For you today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: The City Planning Commission plays a vital role in the long-term growth and development of the city and is paramount to ensuring that it's livable, affordable, equitable, and sustainable, and that it continues to thrive now and in the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Given the significance of this position,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I deeply appreciate this committee's role in evaluating and deciding on this appointment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Members, for your service to the City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I have worked for 36 years as an urban planner in New York, and my career has focused on land use, zoning, development, and preservation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I've held senior positions in both the public and private sectors,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: giving me a broad understanding of and appreciation for

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: how land use decisions are developed, evaluated, and implemented.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Moreover, I believe my decades of leadership experience at three of the city's land use agencies qualifies me to serve on the City Planning Commission.

chapters.summary: Srinivasan details her career at DCP, including Manhattan planning and neighborhood plans, ten years chairing the Board of Standards and Appeals, and four years chairing the Landmarks Preservation Commission, where she cleared a 50-year backlog and introduced online resources.
chapters.title: Srinivasan details DCP, BSA, and LPC leadership

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I began my career in New York in the Manhattan Office of City Planning as an urban planner and liaison to Community Board 5.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Subsequently, as a team leader for Midtown and the Upper East Side and West Side communities, and then as Deputy Director of the Manhattan Borough Office, I directed several major planning initiatives and agency priorities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: My work also involved collaborating with community groups and local civic groups on neighborhood plans, including those for East Harlem and Community Board.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: With Community Board 9 and Civitas, and Central Harlem with Community Board 9, Community Board 10, and the Manhattan Borough President's Office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I then served for 10 years as chair of the Board of Standards and Appeals, overseeing zoning variances, special permits, and appeals applications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: My tenure focused on strengthening professionalism and quality, efficiency, and enhancing transparency in the board's operations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: This included setting higher standards for applications, bringing greater rigor and analytical depth to their review, and creating a more user-friendly website, and for the first time providing access to the board's decisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I also served as the chair of the Landmarks Preservation Commission for four years during my tenure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: LPC advanced a vision centered on good government, equity, efficiency, and access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: We undertook an 18-month public process resolving a 50-year backlog of properties on the Commission's calendar, which resulted in designations across all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: We also implemented preservation priorities in conjunction with the administration's rezoning plans, including in East New York,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: East Midtown, East Harlem, and Gowanus, demonstrating that planning and preservation can go hand in hand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: We initiated reforms to the agency's regulatory processes and introduced online resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Including interactive maps, applicant presentations, commission decisions, and searchable permit databases and digital educational tools.

chapters.summary: Srinivasan describes private-sector work at law firms advising on land use, zoning, and landmarks, which deepened her understanding of property owners, small businesses, and nonprofits. She emphasizes that community boards, elected officials, and stakeholders provide invaluable input.
chapters.title: Srinivasan on private sector and community engagement

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: More recently, I worked in the private sector at two prominent law firms as a senior advisor on land use zoning and landmarks matters within their public strategies and land use practices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: This experience deepened my understanding of the perspective of a property owner, small business, and non-profit organizations, and the challenges they face in program development, financing, and timelines.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Throughout my career, I have worked with community boards and elected officials and civic and business organizations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: At DCP, I engage with community groups on borough-wide proposals and a range of neighborhood plans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: At the BSA, we did extensive outreach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: to reach to community groups, to educate them on the board's mandate, and provide guidance regarding the public process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: At LPC, we collaborated with neighborhood groups on landmark and historic district designations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: As a decision maker and while leading two independent commissions,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I believe it was not only important for community boards, elected officials, and all stakeholders to engage in the process, but their input was invaluable to a robust public review and critical in shaping decisions.

chapters.summary: Srinivasan says she wants to contribute to the CPC amid the housing crisis. She would evaluate applications that advance housing, engage in rigorous public review, respect community boards and Council members, and honor the Commission's independent citywide mandate.
chapters.title: Srinivasan on housing crisis and CPC role

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I am particularly interested in the opportunity to contribute to the Commission at this point of the City's history.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: New York faces significant challenges, including the urgent need for housing, especially affordable housing, as well as neighborhood investment and responsible, sustainable growth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: If appointed, I would welcome the opportunity to evaluate applications that advance the city's overarching goals of addressing the housing crisis, engage in a rigorous public review process, and embrace the responsibilities of this appointment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I believe that the voice of community boards and council members

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I believe the voice are integral to the public review process, and I would approach this responsibility with great respect for their recommendations, while also recognizing that the Commission has been entrusted with an independent citywide mandate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: In summary, if I'm appointed, I would bring to the Commission my leadership,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: and decision-making experience, substantive and technical expertise in planning and zoning, understanding of government processes, and my experience working with communities and other stakeholders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I would also bring my ability to remain independent, understand different points of view, consider a range

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: of changes and modifications to address concerns and make fair and balanced decisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: New York's land use and planning issues have been the focus of my professional life, and I welcome the prospect of returning to public service and contributing to the betterment of the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: My commitment to serve on the Commission is not only professional but deeply personal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: After many years, returning full circle to where I began my career would indeed be like coming home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Ong and members of the committee for your consideration, and I hope to have your support for my appointment.

chapters.summary: Julie Stein thanks the Chair and members and says her family has been in New York for generations, with her grandmother still in Queens and Stein a public school parent in Brooklyn. She studied urban planning, housing policy, fair housing, and earned AICP certification.
chapters.title: Julie Stein opening statement: family and planning background

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Young and members of the Committee on Rules, Privileges, Elections, Standards, and Ethics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: I appreciate the opportunity to appear before you today as you consider my nomination to the City Planning Commission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: I care deeply about New York City, our neighborhoods, and our shared future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: My family has been in New York as long as we've been in this country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: My grandmother, who turns 98 this month, still lives in the Queens apartment that my dad grew up in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: And today, I'm a proud New York City public school parent in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: My interest in urban planning began during my undergraduate studies where I became fascinated with the spatial impact of public policy decisions, in particular the fundamental role

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: that housing policy played in 20th century America's development patterns and the influence that housing had on social welfare outcomes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: That focus led me to pursue my master's in city planning with a focus in housing, community, and economic development, completing an urban design certificate, and writing my master's thesis on fair housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: I obtained my American Institute of Certified Planners certification shortly after graduate school, committing to ongoing professional education to stay at the leading edge of the practice.

chapters.summary: Stein says she spent nearly 20 years in and around city government, including over 12 years at NYCEDC on neighborhood planning and public real estate. She led a business district recovery panel and now serves as Executive Director of the Union Square Partnership.
chapters.title: Stein recounts city government and Union Square Partnership career

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: I've spent nearly 20 years in and around New York City government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: I started my career at City Hall in Health and Human Services and then spent over 12 years at the New York City Economic Development Corporation working on neighborhood planning and managing public real estate assets on behalf of the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: I then served as the executive director of Mayor Adams and Governor Hochul's Joy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: joint blue ribbon panel on business district recovery coming out of the pandemic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: And I now serve as the executive director of Union Square Partnership, the business improvement district, place manager, and community organization for Union Square and 14th Street.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Throughout my career, I've learned that planning in New York is never just a technical exercise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: It's an intensive, collaborative process where stakeholders balance citywide imperatives with local neighborhood needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: I've seen that the most durable planning outcomes happen alongside community participation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: At EDC, whether partnering with Manhattan Community Board 3 to overcome 45 years of deadlock on the Seward Park Urban Renewal Area, or aligning with Bronx Community Board 2 on the Hunts Point Vision Plan, or steering waterfront industrial planning

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: with the Sunset Park Task Force and former council member Carlos Menchaca, working closely with these neighborhood stakeholders yielded better, more implementable projects.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Running a community organization myself now, I bring that ground-level experience to managing our work every day.

chapters.summary: Stein says the city faces an affordable housing crisis and must support commercial corridors, industrial jobs, and climate resiliency. She commits to independent review and public input, and discloses two COIB Rule 1-09 waiver requests related to Union Square Partnership and a potential BID expansion.
chapters.title: Stein on housing crisis, planning role, and COIB waivers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Our city faces a dire affordable housing crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: We must also support thriving commercial corridors and protect our industrial base so New Yorkers have access to good jobs and essential services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: And we must also think about how climate change will impact our city and how to pursue sustainability and resiliency measures to prepare us for the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: The role of a city planning commissioner is to evaluate proposals with independence, objectivity, and a deep respect for public process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: As the commission fulfills its charter-mandated duties, I believe authentic public input remains indispensable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Community boards, council members, and residents provide essential local context, and my obligation will be to carefully weigh that input alongside technical documents such as environmental reviews to ensure that density is always matched with appropriate infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: If confirmed to the CPC, I commit to bringing an analytical, transparent, and grounded perspective to every application before us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: I look forward to working constructively with the council and communities across all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Regarding my nomination and my ongoing role at the Union Square Partnership, two waiver requests of COIB Rule 1-09 have been submitted to the Conflict of Interest Board.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: The first waiver requests permission to allow me to continue to appear before certain city agencies and officials in my role as Executive Director of Union Square Partnership,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: which routinely requires communication with entities named in Rule 1-09, including community boards, council members, and city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: The second waiver request is to allow me to appear before these same named entities in my role as Union Square Partnership Executive Director in relation to the process for a potential expansion of the 14th Street Union Square Business Improvement District.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: I would not appear before the CPC or the Department of City Planning as part of this process, and I would recuse myself from any matter involving Union Square Partnership's bid expansion in my role as City Planning Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Both requests are currently working their way through the formal COIB review process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: I anticipate that COIB will approve these waivers, and I fully commit to abiding by any and all guidance that COIB provides.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your time, and I'm happy to answer questions.

chapters.summary: Margaret Anadu thanks the Chair, Deputy Speaker, and Mayor Mamdani. She grew up between Lagos and Houston, has spent over two decades in New York, and wants to serve because of the housing crisis. Her career has focused on financing affordable housing and community development.
chapters.title: Margaret Anadu opening statement: background and housing focus

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Ung, Deputy Speaker Williams, and members of the Committee on Rules, Privileges, Elections, Standards, and Ethics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Thank you for having me this morning and for this consideration, and thank you to Mayor Mamdani for the honor of this nomination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: My name is Margaret Anadu.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I grew up between Lagos, Nigeria, and Houston, Texas, and I've spent over two decades here in New York, more than half my life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I love big cities, and I love this one most.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I want to serve on this commission for one reason above all, our need for housing, especially affordable housing during this crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: It has been the focus of my career, and so many of the decisions that determine whether New Yorkers can afford to live and thrive here are made at this table.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: My passion for this work and community development more broadly began in Houston.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I was proud of my neighborhood, and I loved my community and my neighborhood, but I was also bused across town to get to a good school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Across town was also where the better stores and amenities were, and even basics like sidewalks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: As a teenager, I didn't understand all of it, but I understood that where you live shapes what you can reach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: For more than 20 years, I've worked on that problem as an investor, financing housing and community development across all five boroughs and in communities nationwide that don't have enough affordable homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Most of that work has been in the private sector as a partner at Goldman Sachs and now at One Weaver, the firm I founded recently, where I work alongside not-for-profits and others to get housing and infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: My investments in hundreds of public-private transactions and my public roles as EDC board chair and briefly with New Jersey Transit gave me glimpses of the other side of the table.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I'd be excited to serve in a new capacity and to bring that perspective with me.

chapters.summary: Anadu calls this a defining moment for housing and says the city must build more housing faster in every borough, with transit-oriented development and thoughtful community engagement. She wants to be a bridge between communities, developers, lenders, and government and will judge applications independently.
chapters.title: Anadu on transit-oriented development and bridge role

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I believe this is a defining moment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Our housing crisis continues to push out the working families who make the city run.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: And the country more than ever now recognizes housing as a national crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: It creates a real opportunity and important responsibility to get it right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Getting it right means getting more done, more housing, faster in every borough, built where the infrastructure can support it and it makes sense.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I believe deeply in transit-oriented development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Partly that's principle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Partly it's that I'm the rare Texan who doesn't know how to drive and doesn't even have a license.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: It also means thoughtful community engagement alongside that work, not in conflict with it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I'd also like to be a bit of a bridge, if possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: In land use, communities, developers, lenders, and government often aren't working from the same information, and that can breed mistrust.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Capital especially is viewed with skepticism, sometimes for good reason.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I've spent my career inside financing decisions, so my perspective includes knowing why one project pencils and another stalls, and what it takes to keep a building affordable from a financial perspective.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: And I'm excited to learn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: From community boards, borough presidents, council members, and my fellow commissioners, hopefully.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: And I'll judge every application with independence on its merits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Where you live shapes what you can reach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I want more New Yorkers to find opportunity right where they live, and I'd be honored to help build that city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Thank you, and I look forward to your consideration and questions.

chapters.summary: Kenneth Knuckles thanks the committee and says public service with competence and integrity is the highest endeavor. He describes decades in New York City government as an attorney, deputy borough president, agency head, and CPC member across five mayoral administrations, and supports balancing affordable housing with neighborhood character.
chapters.title: Kenneth Knuckles opening statement

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Ong, Deputy Speaker Williams, and members of this distinguished committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: And thank you for the opportunity to testify before you today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I am, of course, Kenneth Knuckles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I believe that public service performed with both competence and integrity is the highest of endeavors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Accordingly, that guiding principle has been my North Star.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: are over several decades of experience in New York City government in various capacities as an attorney, a deputy borough president, a city agency head,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
