utterances.text: and of course more recently as a member of the City Planning Commission, a membership that now spans five mayoral administrations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: My continuing interest in land use and city zoning policy stem from my formal education,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: as well as my recognition that rules and corresponding decisions that help shape the city have a profound and lasting impact on the lives of its inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: As a diverse municipality with both high and low-rise communities, urban density, and suburban space, the ongoing quest to find greater opportunities to build affordable housing is both challenging and complex,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: requiring the need to balance demands for more equitable development

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: with preservation of neighborhood character and distinction precious to all of our communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I believe that my experience, gained perspective, and boundless devotion to New York City still render me able to make a meaningful contribution to discussion of the above-mentioned issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: If I should again have the opportunity, I am ready to serve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Ung thanks the candidates, says questions may be directed to all or to individuals, and notes Councilmember Brewer has joined. She asks whether they support coupling housing growth with infrastructure commitments and whether the CPC should secure points of agreement under ELURP.
chapters.title: Chair Ung asks CPC panel about infrastructure and ELURP points of agreement

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you all for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So we're going to start off by, I'm going to ask some questions.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I'm going to ask a password of the committee members.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So when the question is asked, it's not directed toward one person.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: It would be great if all of you could answer it.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And then sometimes you do have questions that will be directed at one person.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: We've also been joined by Council Member Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So I just want to start off the questioning by discussing points of agreement.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: In recent neighborhood rezoning, the City Council has often negotiated points of agreement with the administration to secure infrastructure and capital investment alongside increased density.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Do you support that model of coupling new housing growth with public commitments for infrastructure and other community investments?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Why or why not?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And then the second question, for new eLERP applications, where the city council will no longer play a formal role in the process, should the CBC now attempt to secure points of agreement for local communities?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: If not, what stakeholder is in a position to do that important work?

chapters.summary: Knuckles supports comprehensive planning and leveraging resources for larger projects. He says Council influence remains substantial through community boards and borough presidents, and that ELURP imposes greater responsibility on the CPC to vet environmental and community concerns.
chapters.title: Kenneth Knuckles answers on comprehensive planning and ELURP

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: You guys go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: As the youngest member here, I'll start off.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Well, I believe in...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Comprehensive planning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: And I think comprehensive planning, whether it's led by a city council member or a community board or whatever advocacy emerges from the community, I think is a sound approach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: And I think it

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: is the best vehicle to build consensus quickly or gradually within a given community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: So I believe in comprehensive planning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I do appreciate the fact that larger projects that come before the commission generally have the ability to leverage

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: those kinds of resources from the mayoral administration, as opposed to singular housing projects, major rezonings as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: But I do believe in it, and I have supported it over my years on the commission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: With regard to ELRP, Madam Chair, I believe that was the second part of your question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I appreciate the concerns on the part of the City Council with regard to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: the ELR process and the city planning commission as the supposed final word or say.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: But I know the city council well enough and the dynamic to understand that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: While your role may have been diminished somewhat, your influence will still be substantial, I'm sure, in the ELERP process, certainly as it relates to both the community boards as well as the borough president.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: But I believe that ELERP imposes a greater responsibility on the planning commission members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: To

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: ascertain and make sure from our staff, the staff that testifies before us, that environmental issues, environmental impacts especially,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: and the issues that are raised by both the community boards as well as the borough presidents are vetted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: And seriously considered and resolved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Because if they are not, then the eLERP process will ultimately not have credibility, which is not good for land use in the city and not good for policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I appreciate the fact that the process was voted upon and adopted by the citizenry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: That imposes now the responsibility on the city planning commission to fulfill its mission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: But that mission now will include, I think, a greater scrutiny of the environmental impacts of any project that comes before us in the ELA process.

chapters.summary: Crowell concurs and says infrastructure needs are a key priority. He notes the CPC did not shape the charter revisions but must implement them, and commits to early engagement with affected Council members so community voices shape outcomes and infrastructure priorities.
chapters.title: Anthony Crowell answers on infrastructure and ELURP

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And I concur with my colleague, and I will add that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: understanding the infrastructure needs of our communities is something I identified on my questionnaire to you as a key priority.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I often look at, in my work on the commission, not just what the planning goal is, but understanding what would make it effective in terms of its implementation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And I have concerns, as I think we all do, about infrastructure and infrastructure needs, not just for today, but for tomorrow and planning forward for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And it's critically important that we take steps as a department and as a commission to understand the fullness of that with whatever application is before us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And, of course, environmental review plays a key role in that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: With regard to ELRP,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: The commission did not itself did not play any role in shaping the Charter Revision Commission's proposals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: But now that they have become law, we have the weight of the responsibility of implementing them and implementing them as effectively as possible

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: and understanding their impacts in terms of the procedural changes and the changes in political accountability with regard to the council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: deeply committed, and I've spoken to colleagues on the commission, including the chair, just about making sure that we have a process in place to engage with, as early as possible, council members in affected districts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I think that's critically important to have that dialogue from the outset.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I would anticipate that the kinds of dialogue that take place at the community board level will have an even greater level of council member

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: inclusion and amplification in terms of their perspectives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And I think we need to pay very close attention to that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Obviously, it is a critical moment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: The test of whether our land use processes work well and ensure that community voices are included, particularly council members who represent broad communities, is this moment right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: So I think the commission has that responsibility and it is my personal commitment, but also

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: my commitment as a member of the body that we will all work to ensure that those voices are understood and have a role in shaping the outcomes, including how infrastructure priorities are set.

chapters.summary: Srinivasan supports infrastructure investments alongside rezoning. She distinguishes modest projects from fast-track affordable housing in 12 low-production communities, expects outreach and environmental review to address impacts, and says she will take community and Council input seriously despite no formal role.
chapters.title: Meenakshi Srinivasan answers on infrastructure and ELURP

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Young, for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And I may be repeating myself or repeating what others have said, but I also concur with Anthony and with Ken.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I absolutely believe that planning and rezoning should be accompanied by infrastructure improvements and investments in communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: So that's a sound planning principle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: It's practice that the council has done over decades and has been very successful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And it's really been for the betterment of both communities at the local level, but for the city overall.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: So I support that proposition very much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: In terms of eLIRP, I think there are two types of applications that the commission will entertain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: One are the more modest projects, which have very small increases in density, and those typically do not create controversy or issues in communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: So that's one type of application, but I think what we're talking about here is really the fast-track affordable housing process, which is aimed primarily at

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: the 12 communities that had seen the lowest amount of housing production.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: over the last five years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And I think in those cases, I would make two points.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: One is that for rezonings in those areas, whether they're

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: initiated by the department or by council members, which, by the way, I was very glad to hear that council members are proactively looking at rezoning to their neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: That process or those proposals, I anticipate that there will be a lot of interaction and outreach to communities as well as council members and other elected officials

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: even prior to any kind of filing or before it comes before the commission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: So I think there are a lot of opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: For issues related to the impacts of a proposal or rezoning in a neighborhood to be addressed and already sort of considering different options or different kinds of recommendations of how

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: a proposal can move forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I think in the case of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: the department's initiated rezonings, I would encourage the staff and use whatever levers I have as, if I'm appointed as commissioner,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: to engage with staff to encourage them to continue to do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I think the other thing is that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: if we think about larger rezonings in these neighborhoods, they would also include

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: an environmental review that allows the opportunity to understand what kind of impacts that a proposal may have and also will inform the Commission in terms of what kinds of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: considerations should be given while

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: deliberating on these proposals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: So I think it would address issues related to transportation, sewers, schools,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: the public realm, equity issues, and of course housing affordability and access and economic development and job opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I think that even though the EULA process may not have a formal role for the council and for community boards, I believe it will be anyway integrated in the process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And definitely in terms of a public hearing process, I would really look forward to hear what the community and the council members'position is, as well as take their...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Their issues and recommendations very seriously while deliberating on the project.

chapters.summary: Anadu agrees with her colleagues and says expedited processes make community engagement more important, not less. She says commissioners must consider neighborhood infrastructure and concerns across all applications.
chapters.title: Margaret Anadu answers on ELURP and community engagement

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I appreciate the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I don't want to repeat a lot of what's been said because I actually agree with literally everything that's been said.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I guess one thing I'd like to add is, and I think, Anthony, you touched on sort of the political climate of the moment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I don't think it's lost, hopefully, on anyone that these changes come at a moment where all communities, I think, will be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Heightened to what it looks like to have some of these expedited processes in action and still have their views, their concerns, their voices, quite frankly, heard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: It's certainly something that I know I'm really focused on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I assume all five of us are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: So I think that we will be going out of our way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Despite what specific votes and points in the process don't exist to be taken into account, all of the information we're getting about these neighborhoods, communities,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: the infrastructure that's needed, not specifically just in the moment of a particular application, but in all the discussions we're having across everything that comes before us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: So I am...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Both optimistic about how community engagement can continue to be just, not even just as important as it's been, but quite frankly, even more important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: And I think the changes in whether it's Fast Track, eLURP, et cetera, I think at least for me, make me more

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: heightened to that importance, not less.

chapters.summary: Julie Stein briefly affirms the importance of infrastructure investment commensurate with increased density and concurs with her colleagues' points.
chapters.title: Julie Stein briefly affirms infrastructure and density

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: In the interest of time, I'll say I affirm the importance of infrastructure investment that is commensurate with increased density and that I concur with my colleagues'points.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Riley, the land use chair, says he wants partnership with the CPC and asks what role neighborhood planning should play in producing affordability. He cites his White Plains Road plan and other neighborhood plans that produced thousands of units.
chapters.title: Councilmember Riley questions panel on neighborhood planning and affordability

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I'd like to pass it over to Councilmember Riley.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you to the panel for taking the time to testify with us here today.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I loved a lot of what I heard as land use chair.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I think we're trying to do our best to be as proactive, and we share that deep commitment to actually working together.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And I think that's what we want to focus on.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The notion is that with CPC, there is no going to be working with council, and that's something that we want to make sure that we're addressing.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So just wanted to put that out there, and I love everything that you all said.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Neighborhood zoning, rezoning, my favorite thing now.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I'm doing one in my district, the White Plains Road neighborhood plan.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The council is working on a few neighborhood plans.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: What's the role do you see in neighborhood planning when you're talking about producing affordability within New York City right now?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And I would just add on to this.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I think the issue that I share within the goal is last year we had the deputy speaker who did her neighborhood plan, which we had 12,000 units of housing.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Gowan is 14,000.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So you see that we've achieved a lot of units from neighborhood planning, but it doesn't seem like that is the focus right now with the administration.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So just wanted to get your perspective.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And if I'm wrong, please correct me.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And you all don't have to go if you all share the same sentiments, you can all just add in addition.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: But we'd love just to hear your perspective on neighborhood planning and on how we can utilize that as a tool for addressing affordability.

chapters.summary: Stein says neighborhood planning is critical and that the land use process is only a slice of planning. She says comprehensive looks at capital investment, community infrastructure, and neighborhood needs are important and is heartened by Council and community leadership.
chapters.title: Julie Stein answers on neighborhood planning

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Maybe I can start since I finished the last one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: I mean, as regards to what the administration is thinking, obviously, like, don't have access to a lot of what may not have been publicly shared yet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: But as it relates to my general perspective, I think that neighborhood planning is critical.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: I think, you know, when we talk about ULERP or we talk about what's in front of the City Planning Commission, it's really just a slice of what it looks like to do planning in New York City, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: There are urban planners who do work that's around capital investment, community infrastructure, that may never actually touch a land use process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: And so having a comprehensive look at what a neighborhood needs, up to and including land use, is really important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: And I think that the more leadership that we see on the ground alongside individual actors as well as the public sector are going to result in the best path forward for all of the sort of collective stewardship of a neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: And so I'm really heartened, like my colleague said, about the leadership that we see coming out of.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: council members and we know also community organizations across New York City thinking about what the future of their neighborhoods look like and I think that it's really important that that goes hand in hand

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: with you know whether it's private applications or applications led by the department in order to come up with what our collective future looks like.

chapters.summary: Riley asks Kenneth Knuckles what factors would lead him to vote against a housing proposal. Knuckles says he would vote no if a project does not enhance the built environment, has insufficient affordable units, inadequate environmental analysis, or scale incompatible with the community.
chapters.title: Riley asks Kenneth Knuckles what factors would lead him to vote against housing

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: You guys good with that answer?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: All right, that's fine with me too.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay, this question is directed to Kenneth.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I have actually have a few questions for you, Kenneth.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Apologize to put you on the spot.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: When your pre-hearing response, you emphasize careful review of housing applications as a way to address the housing crisis.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: What factors would lead you to vote against a housing proposal?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Well, at the end of the day, if I vote against a project, it's because I believe that it does not enhance the built environment in that immediate community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Symptomatic of that may be...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Insufficient number of units for affordable housing or an insufficient environmental impact

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: analysis, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: It could be scale of the project in relation to the existing community, although I appreciate that all communities are going to have to look at greater scale if ultimately we're going to achieve the affordable housing that we need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Councilman, if I reach the conclusion that the project does not enhance the community and would have an arguably less than positive effect on the community, then I would vote against it.

chapters.summary: Riley asks what determines whether a neighborhood can accommodate more growth. Knuckles says availability of parcels, industrial and manufacturing areas, and each neighborhood acting in good faith matter; DCP and CPC should facilitate and provide technical assistance while forging consensus with elected officials.
chapters.title: Riley asks Knuckles what determines neighborhood capacity for growth

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Also in your pre-hearing response, you stated that every neighborhood should contribute to addressing the housing crisis.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: What factors determine whether a neighborhood is capable of accommodating more growth?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I think that starts, of course, with the availability of parcels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: And I can remember years ago in our borough, the Bronx, where we had too much city-owned property.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: But it ultimately became the source of the redevelopment of the borough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Which now some 30 years later, I think, has seen a renaissance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: But each neighborhood varies with regard to the availability of land.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: So we've got to look at where the opportunities are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: We've got to look at...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Areas that may be currently zoned industrial and manufacturing to see where housing can be accommodated without extinguishing manufacturing and industrial where it's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: We have

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I think each neighborhood, obviously each community, has got to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I think act in good faith about the need to find affordable housing opportunities where they can, where it can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I think DCP and ultimately the commission must facilitate that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: and bring technical assistance where it's appropriate to communities and to help them, frankly, figure it out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: But we've got to...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Really forge a consensus with elected officials because, you know, you can't really go forward in the face of fervent opposition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: So I think it's a collaborative process.

chapters.summary: Riley notes conflicts with DCP over where density makes sense and asks how Knuckles determines when a project is out of scale. Knuckles says to look at existing zoning and built character, but every community must participate in appropriate upzonings, especially near transit.
chapters.title: Riley asks Knuckles how to determine when a project is out of scale

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Yeah, I definitely believe it's a collaborative process, and I think elected officials are trying to do their job right now.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We're finding specific areas in the communities that make sense where you could produce as much density.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: It does feel like there is conflict when you are talking to DCP regarding some of those parcels in our communities that we believe make a lot of sense to do density opposed to where you guys believe.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And there's tons of examples from me being the zoning chair and land use chair for the last four years where I've experienced that with specific members and DCP.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: In your pre-hearing response, you indicated that balancing the development with neighborhood scale and context was the commission's primary challenge.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: How do you determine when a project is out of scale with a neighborhood?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Well, you look at the existing zoning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: And you look at the...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: the built character of the community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: But as I said, you know, there has to be, I think, participation on the part of every community in terms of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: doing appropriate upzonings where there is...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Certainly where there is mass transit, which has certainly been the focus, I think, of the commission over the last few decades, transit-oriented development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: And we need to scale these projects appropriately as best we can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Now, a number of the projects, as you know, come from or are initiated by private developers who, you know, are not in it to lose money.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: We all know that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I think we...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: My approach has been to understand, I mean, we all live in neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I live in an R5B neighborhood in Wakefield and, you know, a proposal for, well, I would say an R9 building, but that would never happen, obviously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: But, I mean.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: We all are protective of our neighborhoods, but I think we all

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: recognize, hopefully, that if we don't address the affordable housing need in this city, then our neighborhoods are ultimately going to suffer from that.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Riley asks Knuckles about the most urgent challenges with mandatory inclusionary housing. Knuckles discusses debates over affordability levels, MIH level one at 25 percent of square footage at 60 percent AMI, and says greater subsidies yield more units and more city, state, and federal resources are needed.
chapters.title: Riley asks Knuckles about mandatory inclusionary housing challenges

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And last question for you, Ken, before I go to the other panelists.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: You discussed that there are challenges with mandatory inclusionary housing, even though it's been a major accomplishment.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Could you just share what you believe the most urgent challenges with MIHs?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Well, it's a debate that...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Anthony and I have heard, you know, over the last several years, and what is affordable?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: And, you know, whether or not...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: The MIH level one, which starts with 25% of the portion of the building, of the square footage of a building being affordable

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: to those with an AMI of 60% of the city level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: That is, that's the challenge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Fewer, greater subsidies ultimately will yield fewer units.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: So, but.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: The challenge for us is to find, I mean, us as a, we as a city, we've got to find more resources to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: have more people be able to afford housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Now, that comes from the coffers of the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I would hope that in the coming days and years that the federal government will play a bigger role than it's played in recent years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Because we all have our limitations in terms of resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Obviously, the state government is critical to that effort.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: But the challenge continues to be how do we reach as many people as we can with the resources that we have.

chapters.summary: Riley asks Margaret Anadu what zoning changes would most impact housing and what citywide needs are underrepresented. Anadu focuses on process predictability and timing, saying time is money and uncertainty raises costs, and says supportive housing is underrepresented.
chapters.title: Riley asks Margaret Anadu about zoning changes and underrepresented needs

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The next question I have is for Margaret.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Margaret, in your pre-hearing response, you stated that zoning is one of the most powerful tools for addressing housing supply and affordability.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: What zoning changes do you believe would have the greatest impact on housing?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And what citywide needs do you believe are the most underrepresented in the land use decision today?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Thank you so much for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I think, gosh, it's hard to pick one zoning change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I mean, my perspective would really be about

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: process and timing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: You know, coming from the perspective of, you know, thinking there needs to be, I am a pro-development person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I think we need to build a lot more housing, and I think we need to invest a lot in our existing housing stock, and that is just an incredibly...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Capital intensive, you know, endeavor by nature.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: And so I think that the, in some cases, lack of predictability in our processes, the time of our processes, it's just time is money.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Lack of certainty is risk.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: And I think that the more expensive a project gets, the less units you get in total, the less affordable they are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: And so if anything, I would speak to just, you know, efficiency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Predictability time, which I think some of the recent changes will certainly serve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: But of course, it remains to be seen if we can really continue to have the type of community engagement that's really important alongside that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: And then can you remind me the second question?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: What citywide needs do you believe are most underrepresented in the land use decision today?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I guess this, I don't know if this,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: really gets touched in sort of the specificity of the land use process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I know it certainly can come through some of the community benefits agreements I've seen, but I would say the need for supportive housing in conjunction and in concert with our affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Riley asks Anthony Crowell how the CPC should measure success on the housing crisis. Crowell says measure total production, depth and permanence of affordability, neighborhood context, and infrastructure; he supports MIH but wants more research on AMI levels and constant innovation.
chapters.title: Riley asks Anthony Crowell how CPC should measure housing success

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Anthony.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: In your pre-hearing response, you identified affordable housing production as the Commission's most pressing challenge.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: How should the Commission measure success in addressing that housing crisis?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Thanks for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I think that...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Over time, we need to look at total housing production and depth of affordability, which Ken was talking about, and with that depth, the permanence of affordability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And then, of course, really consider how we're being successful while appreciating neighborhood context.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Ensuring that the proper infrastructure is there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And as we move forward, use different project areas as models for how to have a more effective citywide build out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I think that it's critically important that we have

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: some indicators that show that the tools we're using are successful, but also I think we have to just

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Do constant innovation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I'm very committed to ensuring that MIH is as successful as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: and can raise some issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I would like to do more research and understanding how effective using AMI is right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I am not entirely sure when I see certain AMI levels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I'm like, that can't be.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Doesn't make sense, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And I'd like to understand that a little more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: So that's on the other side, doing more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Greater understanding of the research and where that research is coming from.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And so it's a comprehensive suite of things, both performance indicators and innovation and research on a forward-looking basis.

chapters.summary: Riley asks whether Bloomberg-era downzonings should be reconsidered. Crowell says nothing should be off the table during a housing crisis, but history and context matter; he says he remains open-minded and objective in reviewing land use decisions.
chapters.title: Riley asks Crowell about Bloomberg-era downzoning and evolving views

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Two more questions for you, Anthony.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So in your pre-hearing response, you stated that many of Bloomberg-era downzoning reflected legitimate concerns at the time, while also acknowledging today's housing crisis.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Looking back, do you believe any of those downzoning should be reconsidered?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I think that we have a housing crisis right now and that there should be a situation where nothing is off the table in terms of their review.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: But it's always interesting and important to understand the context and how initial decisions were made and how we progress from them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: So I would look at any application, look at any neighborhood proposal, and want to understand

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: its history, of course, but also what can we achieve in terms of the crisis that we're trying to manage forward.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So is it safe to say your views have evolved during your tenure on the commission?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I am always open.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: open-minded absolutely in terms of what could be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I think when you're looking at land use, you have to make sure you're keeping that open mind and looking at everything objectively and with an eye towards understanding how to solve problems.

chapters.summary: Riley asks Meenakshi Srinivasan what a reasonable certification time frame is and how to measure process reforms. Srinivasan says balance quality and delay, charter changes allow staff redeployment, environmental review was the biggest stumbling block, and SEQRA changes may streamline review.
chapters.title: Riley asks Srinivasan about certification time frames and process reforms

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And the last question is for Minoski.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: In your pre-hearing response, you identified delays in pre-certification and project review as one of the Commission's biggest challenges.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: What do you believe is a reasonable time frame for certifying an application, and how should the Commission measure whether recent process reforms are actually succeeding?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member, for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I need to think.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: So what would be an ideal amount of time?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I think there are two issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: One is that you want to ensure that the quality of applications and the information needed to be

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: for an application to be filed and certified is not diminished based on the period of time of pre-application review.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And I think balancing that is that it doesn't go on extensively and to the point where it really frustrates both applicants as well as people in the community who are waiting for investments in their neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I think that what we'll see now that there have been changes to the charter, I think that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: will allow the commission to and staff to sort of reorganize and deploy staff differently in terms of the review process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And I understand that the chair has, and the administration is looking at speed and sprint and various mechanisms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: But I think the intent, if I remember correctly, is something for something like six months, which otherwise would take

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: you know, two, two and a half to three years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: So the delays were based on, I think, a couple of things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: One is the number of applications that go through.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I think the complexity of those applications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I think the environmental review was probably the biggest stumbling block.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And I worked on the other side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: With clients and bringing applications before city planning, and it was the environmental review that was really problematic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: So some of the changes to SEEKR is going to also be able to streamline the process, and I think it'll do two things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Again, it's not only the process for applications that may be exempt from SEEKR, but also staff that worked on those or would have worked on those applications can be redeployed to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: make the application or pre-application process much more efficient.

chapters.summary: Riley closes by saying investments are tied to unit count and the city needs to be affordable and livable. He notes infrastructure concerns in his district, urges better messaging about neighborhood plans, and says waterfront development is a major opportunity.
chapters.title: Riley closes with remarks on investments, messaging, and waterfronts

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And just want to end with this.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I love everything you guys said.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I'm looking forward to partnering here and partnering with you guys.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Just want to emphasize that.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: It does seem like investments are always tied to unit count.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And I think that's the issue that we're seeing now where we want to talk about not only having an affordable New York City, but a livable New York City.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Kenneth lives in my district.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure he wouldn't want me to add density there without taking care of the infrastructure issues that are happening within our community as well.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And I think that's what a lot of communities are seeing, and that's what members are seeing as well.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Lastly, messaging.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I live in a highly residential community with a lot of homeowners, and they don't understand the concept of why we have to produce our neighborhood plan in my district right now, because we haven't done a great job with the messaging

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: and letting people understand that there's population change, there's new needs that we have to focus on.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So I do think messaging.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And lastly, waterfronts.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I do think we have a tremendous opportunity to activate a lot of our waterfront because that's where we're losing a lot of our New Yorkers to New Jersey, parts of Connecticut, because they are prioritizing building on those waterfronts.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So those three notions just for you guys to heed in.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And thank you so much for the opportunity, Chair.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Banks reviews the candidates' pre-hearing answers on community benefits agreements and asks when CBAs are necessary to protect communities from the externalities of proposed development projects.
chapters.title: Councilmember Banks questions panel on community benefits agreements

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I'd like now to pass it over to Councilmember Banks.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I want to, first of all, discuss the community benefits agreements.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And we know that via community benefits agreements, council members have been able to get

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: affordability and make major infrastructure investments or commitments to infrastructure investments.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: In our pre-hearing questions, we asked all five candidates to explain under what circumstances, if any,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Are CBAs necessary to protect communities from the externalities of proposed developments?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Cornwell answered that CBAs can be a valuable tool in planning, but their necessity...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And what they look like depends on the individual project.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And that there is no cookie-cutter approach.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Srinivasan, I hope I'm not butchering your name.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Answered that there may be circumstances where CBAs are appropriate, but their use depends on the project itself.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Margaret, your response, you answered that there may be examples where private CBAs have been productive.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: But private enforcement carries risk.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And so here, her preference is for key commitments to be made publicly and enforced by the public sector.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And Mr.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Stein.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You answered that CBAs are not under the purview of the CPC because the CPC applications are evaluated on land use rationale and

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: the formal public record.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And Mr.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Knuckles answered that CBAs are not within the jurisdiction of the CPC, and nor should they be.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: While CBAs may fall outside the formal land use purview of the commission,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: The underlining question remains how the city can ensure that growth is accompanied by the infrastructure and investments necessary to support it.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I would like you all to expand on your answers.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Under what circumstances, if any, would a CBA be necessary to protect communities from the externalities of proposed development projects?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: If you can all expand on your answer.

chapters.summary: Margaret Anadu says agreements between parties can be productive, but she prefers key commitments to be enforced publicly rather than through private agreements, which carry heightened enforcement risk.
chapters.title: Margaret Anadu answers on community benefits agreements

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I'm happy to start and thank you for the important question and for reminding us all what we said so we can be consistent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I think that any agreement between two bodies can be productive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: My comment about a slight...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Preference for the infrastructure that we think is crucial and necessary and you know part of a set of circumstances why we think a particular you know land use application makes sense

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: my thought was that as much as possible those things should be enforced clearly

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: by the public sector body that approve the circumstances by which the community benefits agreement is necessary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: So my one comment and remarks was just about a heightened risk, I think, in private agreements that can only be enforced privately.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I just believe there's risk there.

chapters.summary: Srinivasan says projects that do not go to the Council mean the CPC must grapple with infrastructure, schools, open space, and tenant protections. She says commitments should be incorporated into capital plans or backed by agency feedback.
chapters.title: Meenakshi Srinivasan answers on community benefits agreements

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And I'm happy you asked about CBAs because I've tried to educate myself a little bit since the time that I submitted the questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And I think one

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: One of the things is I would agree with the sentiment that there are certain projects that will be before the City Planning Commission and will not go to the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And that's where the City Council has often negotiated investments in their neighborhood for infrastructure, for schools, open space, tenant protections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: You know, conceptually it really does fall on the commission to grapple with those issues as we consider land use applications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I would say that, you know, the CBA is, I guess CBA is a sort of an instrument that's used.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And, um,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Instead of commenting on that instrument, there may be another instrument that should be used, but I think your point is, and what I feel that the Commission should ensure, is that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: investments are committed in some form or manner, whether it's actually getting some feedback from department heads,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: who are committing to that, whether it's incorporated into a capital plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And, you know, I believe that Chair Sherman even noted that, that there are tools that are available, that the department intends to use all these levers and tools that can, in fact,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: address the issues of impacts and effects in the neighborhood and be able to mitigate any added density or growth in neighborhoods.

chapters.summary: Knuckles says CBAs can benefit communities, but the CPC should stay in its lane by evaluating project merits and impacts rather than negotiating resources beyond the project. He says elected officials may not favor the CPC carving out CBAs.
chapters.title: Kenneth Knuckles answers on community benefits agreements

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Knuckles?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: And I certainly believe that where community benefits agreements can be negotiated and carved out, I think they're for the good of communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: My perspective in terms of the city planning commission's role was or is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: That I think we should more or less stay in our lane.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: In terms of looking at a city planning application, I think it's our role, obviously, to determine

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: the merits of the project and critique the impact of a project on a community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: And speak to whatever deficits we see.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: But in terms of community benefits agreements, I don't think it necessarily the role of the City Planning Commission to negotiate with applicants about resources over and above

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: what the project presents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Because I think that creates issues that take us beyond, arguably, what our role should be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: And I think, frankly, institutionally, I don't know that elected officials would look kindly upon the city plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Planning Commission carving out CBAs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I just think it could be problematic.

chapters.summary: Stein says CBA framing assumes a project is external and hostile. She believes projects are most successful when comprehensively integrated into the community from the start, citing the Seward Park/Essex Crossing collaborative process.
chapters.title: Julie Stein answers on community benefits agreements

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you for your response, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Stein.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Thank you so much for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: I'll speak to both my pre-hearing response, but also to align just my perspective on this philosophically with what I mentioned in my response to Councilmember Riley's question before.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: I think that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: The idea of a CBA often comes with the assumption that a project is swooping in as an outside action and that it is not of the community or it's not integrated with the community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: So the idea is that there's some project, it has a number of impacts, and they have hostile impacts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: They have impacts that...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Can only be mitigated through some sort of agreement with the community where they, you know, get some sort of commitments that counterbalance the impacts of the project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: But philosophically, going again back to what I mentioned to Councilmember Riley, I believe that these projects are the most successful when they're thought of comprehensively in the sense of, within the vein of like overall neighborhood stewardship.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: And I think whether it's a private application or work that is being brought from the department, that these are projects that should be thought of as how they are

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: comprehensively good and well-designed and integrated into the community from the get-go, as opposed to a project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: that has these negative externalities that then need to be mitigated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: So you'll see when you have information that comes back through an environmental review, thinking about potential impacts and potential mitigations, those are not a give and take.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Those are things that get integrated back into the project fundamentally, whether it's an infrastructure investment or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: And I take the same perspective here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: I take it from the work that I did over...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Many years working on the public side, but I'll just, I'll give one example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: So the first project that I worked on when I was at EDC was the Seward Park Urban Renewal Area project, which, you know, became Essex Crossing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: But that wasn't, you know, for many years, 45 years, the city had come and said, we want to do this version of this project, we want to do that version of this project, we want to do this other version, and they always got shot down because they were not of the community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: The innovation that happened in 2010 or 2007, 2008, 2009, and finally in 2010 was

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: going through an intensive collaborative process with the community board, with the council member, with different members of the community to say, hey, community board,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: come up with a set of guidelines that we'll build a project around.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: And it turned what had been an incredibly controversial and really impossible roadblock into a project that was able to be built.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: And I think my lessons from that are that there are ways to position projects so that they are comprehensively thoughtful about the way they integrate into the community as opposed to something that flies in and has to mitigate its impacts.

chapters.summary: Crowell acknowledges the CPC's jurisdictional boundaries. He says CBAs can be important and sometimes necessary for a project to gain support, but the CPC does not arbitrate fairness; it hears concerns through testimony, especially from Council members.
chapters.title: Anthony Crowell answers on community benefits agreements

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Crowell.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Thanks for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: So I'll just say at the outset that I do want to acknowledge the jurisdictional boundaries between what the CPC does and the role that community benefits agreements play and how they're negotiated on a more community and political level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Let me just say that I think that community benefits agreements play an important role.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Sometimes without them, a project can't go forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And that's a value that we have to understand and appreciate and understand how projects evolve from having community, not having community support to ultimately having community support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: We hear those perspectives and that's important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: So I think it's important that we understand the.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: That we recognize the value of them and understand that CPC does not arbitrate what is a just or fair community benefits agreement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: We may hear its justness and fairness through the voice of those who testify before us, the council members in particular.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: So is that helpful?

chapters.summary: Banks asks how the city determines whether supporting infrastructure investments are adequate. Crowell says rely on DCP staff and agency partners, environmental review, and formal processes. Anadu agrees and adds public testimony.
chapters.title: Banks asks how city determines supporting infrastructure adequacy

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you for your responses.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And I guess this particular question, these two lines of questions, anyone can choose to answer.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: When evaluating significant new housing development, how should the city determine whether supporting infrastructure investments are adequate?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I can start.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Yeah, you can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I think it's critically important that we rely on both the work of the department staff, which is exceptional, and equally as important and exceptional are the work of the agency partners we have, depending on the nature of the infrastructure in question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And I think those are fundamental threshold analyses that we look to, of course, environmental review and the formal processes, but it all plays into that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: So that's a really critical.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Critical component.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Critical component.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Did you want to chime in?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I mean, I agree with all that and just an importantly public testimony.

chapters.summary: Banks asks when the CPC would use tools to protect local interests. Knuckles says CPC evaluation, findings, diligence, staff critique, and project withdrawals protect communities, and he is open to hearing additional perspectives.
chapters.title: Banks asks when CPC would use tools to protect local interests

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: To the extent that the CPC has or is developing tools to protect local interests, in what instances would the CPC use those tools?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Well,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I'd like to think that in our evaluation of projects and their suitability and their compliance with

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: existing zoning or in the case of zoning changes that the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: the various findings that we must make.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I think that process hopefully is protective of the community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I think our diligence in looking at these cases, not cases, but applications,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: and using our best judgment, which encompasses knowledge of communities, and obviously the record before us, and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: inquiries with our staff, which we hold to high standards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: And I'd also mention, you know, there are projects that don't make the cut within the commission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I mean, in many cases, they're withdrawn based on critique of staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: So I think...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Performing our due diligence is hopefully protective of communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: But if there are ways or perspectives that need greater appreciation, then I am all for hearing them.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Did anybody else want to chime in on that?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.
