chapters.summary: Banks asks Crowell which infrastructure systems concern him most as housing production increases. Crowell lists water, sewer, transportation, roadway capacity, open space, and schools, and says lower-production areas may lack infrastructure.
chapters.title: Banks asks Crowell which infrastructure systems concern him most

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: This specific question is towards Mr.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Corral.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: In your pre-hearing response, you identified infrastructure as a major concern.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Which infrastructure systems concern you most as housing production increases?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Water, sewer, concerned about transportation, access to public transportation, roadway capacity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Open space, obviously schools.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: So those are a variety of types of infrastructure that should all be considered.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And certainly as we look to certain areas that have had lower production, it's always important to ask why.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And there might be a why that lies in some of the infrastructure availability.

chapters.summary: Banks asks Knuckles which infrastructure systems concern him and how the city should prioritize investments. Knuckles cites water and sewer capacity, schools, and open space, and says comprehensive planning is necessary to address infrastructure impacts in growing neighborhoods.
chapters.title: Banks asks Knuckles about infrastructure concerns and prioritization

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you for that response.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Knuckles, in your pre-hearing response, you identified affordable housing and infrastructure as key challenges.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Which infrastructure systems concern you most as housing production increases?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And how should the city prioritize infrastructure investments in growing neighborhoods?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Well, there is water and sewer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I mean, we're an old city, so where you bring thousands of units into a community, there's got to be strict attention paid to the capacity of that community to sustain

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: those units.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: There are schools, obviously the impact on school seats, and there is open space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Some communities, too few probably in New York City, but some communities have more than an abundance of open space and others don't have sufficient.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: areas of open space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: So it's comprehensive planning when and where you can do it that's necessary to really address the infrastructure impact.

chapters.summary: Banks asks Srinivasan what infrastructure investments are most critical when adding housing. Srinivasan lists school seats, open space, transit capacity, and the public realm, saying priorities depend on location and application. Asked about parking, she says parking is not infrastructure but needs exist and alternatives are needed.
chapters.title: Banks asks Srinivasan about critical infrastructure investments

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you for your response on that.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And for Mrs.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Srinivasan, in your pre-hearing response, you emphasized the importance of securing infrastructure investments alongside growth.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What types of infrastructure investments do you view as most critical when adding new housing?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Water, sewer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Seem like that's the...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: With added density, I think there's a host of infrastructure that we should be looking at.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: School seats, we should look at open space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Capacity for transportation or transit, the public realm as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: So I think identifying which infrastructure needs are important is related to the location, the community, and the type of application or proposal that's

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: That's before the commission.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Is parking also one of those things you look at too as well?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Because I know my district.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I personally wouldn't say parking is infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I understand that there are parking needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Often that's incorporated and required.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Even with the new zoning taking place, they still require parking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I think...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: As a more sort of philosophical issue, I think the idea is that communities should become more sustainable, so should have options that don't require only usage of a car.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: So it would be good, in fact, if other buses and other transports also alleviates the parking demand.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Well, driving a car is an option, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Ung follows up on how the CPC works with the School Construction Authority when school seats are needed. Anadu says it requires comprehensive planning and heightened attention in relevant applications, and that the CPC must consider but may not force a developer to create seats.
chapters.title: Chair Ung follows up on SCA school seats and CPC authority

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you, Gia.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Actually, I do have one follow-up question about this infrastructure because I forgot.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Someone did answer working with the other agencies in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So, for example, I'll give an example, like SCA, right, School Construction Authority, because we just talked about the need for, you know, infrastructure in any development.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And, you know, school seats right now are, you know, important.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: How do you actually see that relationship working out?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So in terms of, you know, SCA saying, you know, in this neighborhood, we really do need to get more seats.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: For the neighborhood because of the development.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: What would your responses be to that if that is a concern of SCA, something that the community does need?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Anyone could answer this question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I think it's, thank you for the specific question and tying those things together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I mean, I think it's consistent with sort of some of the comments you've been hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: It's a part of really important comprehensive planning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: So I think if there's a, you know, so much of this exercise feels like how you get

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: you know, efficiently, accurately, productively, all of the right information to make these really complex decisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: So in a scenario where SCA has been fairly specific about a geography, a neighborhood where there are not enough seats, then that would just be something that requires really heightened attention in any land use application that's relevant in that community.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: What would the response be if, you know, sometimes, you know, I get it, you know, feedback saying that, but, you know, CPC doesn't really have the ability to, you know, ask the developer in that situation or to,

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I'm going to use the word force, but to make a developer, you know, to, you know, put that as a part of the, you know, of the project.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: What would your response be to that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I mean, I should lean on the two guys who've been here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: But I will say, I mean, I think that is one data point that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: if overwhelmingly there is a perspective that there are, you know, severely not enough seats relative to a proposal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: is requiring significant or sort of proposing significant additional density, then that would be a really important consideration amongst all the other factors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: So I don't know that, I guess I wouldn't take it as we don't have the appropriate privity to say you need to create more seats, but we have the, not just privity, but the obligation to take that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: factor into account in what's being proposed and respond appropriately.

chapters.summary: Knuckles says if an SCA assessment shows inadequate school seats and a project would exacerbate the shortage, he would be duty-bound not to approve it. He says the better approach is to advocate for more school seats so the city does not choose between seats and bedrooms.
chapters.title: Kenneth Knuckles answers on school seats and infrastructure

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, and I agree with my colleague, my soon-to-be colleague, hopefully.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: No, if I am aware of an SCA assessment that there's an inadequacy of seats in a

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: given community and there's a project coming forward before us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: And in most cases, you know, developers, unless they're doing several thousand units, I don't think you can negotiate with the developer about school seats.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: So it's incumbent upon the SCA and city government to provide those school seats.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Again, I think I said earlier in an earlier response, if there's an inadequate, if there's an environmental impact that states that there's a shortage of schools and there's a project

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: that's arguably going to exacerbate that shortage, then I think we're duty bound, certainly I would be, to not approve a project that would have such a negative impact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: But I think the more positive approach would be to advocate for

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: more seats on the part of the school system so that we don't have to choose between seats and bedrooms.

chapters.summary: Williams says her neighborhood plan was told no new school seats were needed despite overcrowding and urges commissioners to interrogate agency criteria. She asks whether the panel agrees culture and art should be treated as infrastructure.
chapters.title: Williams questions school seat criteria and culture as infrastructure

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I'd like to pass it off now to our Deputy Speaker Williams.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thanks, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I just want to say for my neighborhood plan, they told me that we

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: didn't have a need for new school seats.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And when I asked them, like, what criteria they used to, like, present that information, they didn't really have anything substantive.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So I also hope that as commissioners that you question the validity of some of these

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: recommendations from the agency because I didn't really understand or believe or trust that the criteria that they use to make a determination that we don't need additional school seats was accurate.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So I just want to say that because many of the schools that are within the neighborhood plan are all at capacity.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Like every single one either has been expanded or currently under expansion.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so if you have schools right in the vicinity that are currently expanding because they're over capacity,

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: How is it that when you think about building new units that you say there's not going to be a need for new school seats?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So I just wanted to say that, that they told me I did not need new school seats, and I did not agree with that, and I did not agree with the criteria that they used to make an assessment.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: to say we don't think you'll need new school seats in 10 to 15 years.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I know overall in New York City, school enrollment in New York City public schools is down, and I know that's a part of the calculation, but again, I hope that you question what is presented to you

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: and truly interrogate the validity of some of these recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I have a random question and then real questions.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So also I'm chair of cultural affairs, and one of the things I've been talking to many of the cultural institutions and advocates about is this idea of culture as infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so when we talked about infrastructure, of course, many people say sewer water.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Like that is what we think about when we think physical infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But it is my belief that culture and art should be a part of how we plan for communities.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And it should also be looked at with the same importance as physical infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So just wanted to know if you agree with that, what you think about culture as infrastructure, because I do think it's important in terms of how we plan for our communities.

chapters.summary: Knuckles cites the 125th Street rezoning, which requires 5 percent of large projects to be devoted to a cultural institution. He says similar approaches can be considered elsewhere to enhance cultural infrastructure.
chapters.title: Kenneth Knuckles answers on culture as infrastructure

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Well, I'll go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I would just say, believe it or not, I'm old enough to remember the rezoning of 125th Street, which was 2008.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: And as a part of that zoning legislation and code, if you build within certain boundaries of 125th Street, if you build...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: A project that is at least 60,000

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: square feet, then 5% of it must be devoted to a cultural institution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: That was in recognition of and in furtherance of the 125th Street corridor as a cultural corridor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I think that approach

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: in appropriate scale, you know, can and should be looked at in other venues in the community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Jamaica just has a strong cultural heritage and virtually every, you know, every, every,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: one of our boroughs and communities within it have it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: But that's one approach to zoning that I think enhances the cultural infrastructure within a given community.

chapters.summary: Williams asks about leveraging air rights for cultural institutions. Crowell notes that the new Civil Rights Museum opened as a benefit of the 125th Street zoning.
chapters.title: Williams follows up on air rights and cultural institutions

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I should have spoke to you because DCP gave me a hard time.

utterances.text: We've got some money for some of the cultural institutions, but we really try to be creative with air rights.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: That's good to know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Hopefully you'll be there Saturday morning when the

utterances.text: They opened the new Civil Rights Museum, which is, as a benefit of that exact zoning, one of my private sector favorites.

chapters.summary: Stein supports treating culture as infrastructure, citing community-use opportunities and libraries. She notes 23 years on the Brooklyn Public Library board and five years as chair, and Williams thanks her for mentioning libraries.
chapters.title: Julie Stein comments on cultural infrastructure and libraries

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: More comments on this question?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: If you have anything else to add.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: When we had that nice conversation a few weeks ago, I appreciated you bringing that up, and it's something that I fully support along the same lines as Ken and reflecting what went on in 125.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: That is a key cultural infrastructure for all of Brooklyn and adapting in real time to make sure library service is available, but also the kinds of programming that our cultural program is essential.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: So it should be a clear part of our planning process.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And thanks for mentioning the libraries.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: They're also part of my committee.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Don't want them to think I forgot about them.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: It's all packaged.

chapters.title: Meenakshi Srinivasan answers on ELURP and community board recourse

utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.text: I just want to clarify my answer.

utterances.text: I think the first question was what recourse, and I said Article 78.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I think that was really sort of a legal answer to the fact that if the commission approved a project and the community wanted to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: appeal it is somewhere it would have to go to an article 78 so that's just a legal answer but if if your question is more so that

utterances.text: the commission is moving in a particular direction they're not listening to the voices that the the community board has raised

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I think that's a different question, and I'm happy to answer that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I feel that if I'm appointed to the commission, I think it's absolutely imperative to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: hear what the concerns are during the process and deliberate with the commissioners, with the chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I've led to agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: We always heard different voices from a spate of stakeholders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And I think we often, in fact, more often than not, try to negotiate, not negotiate,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: We deliberate, let's say, an outcome that address those concerns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: So we use the tools that are available, which is whether we should modify projects to address the concerns, whether we should impose conditions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: So I believe that even in the commission, one can explore the tools that can try and address concerns that we hear from community boards and from elected officials.

chapters.summary: Stein says community board recommendations have always been advisory but are taken seriously and remain so under ELURP. Anadu says she agrees word for word.
chapters.title: Julie Stein and Margaret Anadu answer on community board recommendations

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: In my experience, even though community board recommendations have always been advisory, they're always taken extremely seriously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: And nothing about that changes through the ELIP process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: You know, of course, while both council members and community boards are representative of local community,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: I've always seen the community board recommendations play out as an important thing of its own, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Not necessarily tied later on in the council process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: And so, you know, I'm pleased that the community boards will retain that key opportunity for giving their advisory recommendation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: And then, of course, having community members and...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Council members and representatives of the community board will be able to testify throughout the rest of the process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Literally agree word for word with what Julie just said.

chapters.summary: Knuckles says ELURP was about time management, not making approvals easier, and places a greater burden on the CPC to address environmental and community board issues. He says community boards are sophisticated about land use and must be taken seriously.
chapters.title: Kenneth Knuckles answers on ELURP and community boards

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: No, I would just say, with regard to ELRP,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I think the impetus for E-Lert was not to, certainly I don't perceive it to be, to make it easier to get through E-Lert.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: It was about time management.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: But as I said earlier, I think it places an even greater burden

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: on CPC to make sure that environmental impacts and other issues that are raised by

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: the community boards and the borough president are addressed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I mean, they're going to be substantive, and as they are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I think community boards in the city of New York are very, very sophisticated about land use because, frankly,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: That's where they probably have the most impact over and above, you know city services and Those are the issues that that frankly raise the ire of local communities mostly so

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: They have to be taken seriously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: They are and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: And I think.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I think it places a greater burden and responsibility on the Planning Commission to make sure what we

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: evaluate and ultimately approve is really in the best interest of the community in a given instance.

chapters.summary: Williams says community board sophistication varies and some boards need better education on land use projects so the CPC can assess input equitably.
chapters.title: Williams comments on community board capacity and education

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I will say that from my experience, even being on the community board, the experience is layered.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I think some community boards, even when we get back, and I'm sure you see it with the community board responses, some community boards are very sophisticated and have very substantive recommendations that you can say, okay, maybe we can tweak things here and there.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And then there are community boards that don't.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I don't know if this is like maybe community boards need better education when land use projects are coming to their community board.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: That would just be my only flag that I do think the ways in which community members make their voices heard, it's not always equitable across community boards in ways that allow for

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: true assessment from the CPC.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So just something to consider.

chapters.summary: Williams asks how the CPC can ensure community benefits and outreach for projects reviewed through ELURP, noting that many people do not engage at CPC and entry points will differ.
chapters.title: Williams asks how CPC can ensure community benefits and outreach under ELURP

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: For neighborhood projects that go through ULERP, local council members, and I think we've been talking about this with my colleagues here, as you know, often play a crucial role in securing project modifications, local investments, or other community benefits in order to ensure the proposal

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: will not have adverse impact.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: impacts on the local community.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: How can the commission help ensure similar community benefits are achieved for projects reviewed through eLRP?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And just one thing I wanted to add to this idea of, you know, what can the commission do around community benefits is

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: how can they ensure that there is outreach to community members?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so I'm thinking about my neighborhood plan.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Like, there was a decent amount of people that testified.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I honestly felt like there could have been more people that testified on the neighborhood plan.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But my office.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Physically picked up the phone and asked people to call and we had been going through a process of a steering committee

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: that informed the plan so there was a lot of engagement along the way but I just personally feel like

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: A lot of people don't really come to CPC.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I know in my conversations with you all, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Crow, I remember you saying, like, a lot of, you know, you guys were happy to see me, but a lot of council members also don't come to the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so I feel like maybe it's on our end, and maybe we need to talk to our land use folks.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But also just from your end, how are we ensuring that people actually engage at the right entry points?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Because the entry points are going to be significantly different for eAlert projects.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So I know it's like layered.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So engagement, but like the engagement in terms of ensuring that like these can.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: community concerns are being addressed.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But to me, you can't even really address community concerns if people don't even know that they have an opportunity to talk about the community concerns.

chapters.summary: Stein says civic engagement is also infrastructure and that the city should invest in community organizations and networks before land use processes. Long-term stewardship, she says, yields better engagement.
chapters.title: Julie Stein answers on civic engagement as infrastructure

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: So, you know, building off of what you mentioned before about arts and cultures being infrastructure, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Civic engagement is also infrastructure, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: And there's a lot of...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Muscle memory that gets built over years before you're ever in front of a land use process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: And so I think it is incumbent upon us, whether, you know, both at the community level, at the city level,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: to be investing in community organizations and processes that are, frankly, have nothing to do with land use because it builds the networks and the ecosystems that allow us to engage people more thoroughly when something like this comes up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: I started the day saying that, you know, planning is a lot more than a land use application.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: And I've worked, you know, over almost 20 years in this and only done a few land use applications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: I think you...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Will get the best type of engagement, like you're mentioning, when you have organizations who are, you know, further able to work with their people to bring them in, when there are elected officials who are hyper-engaged.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Also, when we think about

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: This is a long-term stewardship process that is outside of any application.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: And so I would just sort of like piggyback on the idea of cultures and infrastructure to say civic engagement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: When we do it right across the board, benefits specific instances like land use.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: strengthens our city overall.

chapters.summary: Knuckles notes that CPC hearings occur during work hours and that community boards are key venues. He says the city should use technology and community media to communicate hearings and increase input.
chapters.title: Kenneth Knuckles answers on hearing times and technology outreach

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: You know, I would just say, as it relates to the City Planning Commission, you know, review sessions and public hearings on Mondays and Wednesdays

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: happen in the morning and in the afternoon when most of the people who are impacted by our decisions are working.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: And that's not going to change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Obviously, you know, community boards are aware, at least.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Presumably, that's where the neighborhoods can really come and let their voices be heard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: But I think, you know, in this age of media, and I'm sure you're more sophisticated in this area than I, but we have to do more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: We have to do more to, I think, use technology to...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Communicate with our communities, as well as the community-based programming, the local, you know, our local stations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Bronx, what is it called in the Bronx?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I forgot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Yeah, the community-based channels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I think they...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I think they ought to be utilized to the maximum effect to communicate when hearings are going to take place and what the hearings are going to be about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: And I would presume that the department would facilitate that in any way because at the end of the day, the more

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: the more input we have, I think the better informed our decision-making process is.

chapters.summary: Stein adds that social media from elected officials can reach people personally and objectively, shape perceptions of projects, and invite engagement in ways that work for residents.
chapters.title: Julie Stein adds on social media outreach

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Yeah, I just want to piggyback on what was said, and I'll just add I do think there's an opportunity to think about using that new media to reach people, particularly social media.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Social media from elected officials can be a very powerful tool.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: It can present items in an objective way, but also a way that is personal because it affects where they live.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: And in addition, it can help shape.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: The public's perception of projects that are being proposed, applications that are being made, and inviting people to engage, and sometimes engage in the way that works best for them, but so that you as their representative can hear

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: their voice and community boards can hear their voice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: So I think those are some, some,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: It's hard to reach people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: So using as many of these strategies as possible and being able to cut through and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: a lot of different noise is really important and a way to engage people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: But I find that if you don't engage people where they want to be engaged or are willing to be engaged, it doesn't work.

chapters.summary: Williams asks whether commissioners have authority to ensure engagement happens and whether hearing times can be more accessible. Stein says DCP uses social media, its website, remote links, and staff outreach, but alternate timing requirements are unclear.
chapters.title: Williams asks about authority to ensure engagement and accessible timing

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, and I mean, that was a challenge for us during the neighborhood plan.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So in your roles, do you have the authority to...

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Ensure that these forms of engagement do happen and like even what you said about the timing for the hearings is it like does it have to be in the morning like

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: can there be proposal even if it was like once a month or once that like I mean I don't know how it really works but like are there opportunities to make

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: it more accessible for every single New Yorker to be engaged in the land use process, shall they wish?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: So I will give huge props to the department and the commission for using social media in what I think has been very effective ways to educate the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Using the website, directing people from social media to the website.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Even they recently created a little book for children on the land use process, which I found really nice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: So there's capacity to be creative and to innovate in outreach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: I also think that when it comes to accessibility,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: We should note, even though some of those hearings are during the daytime, it is possible for people to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: participate via remote links at lunchtime.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: There are times when people can come in and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: There are no shortage of people who participate, particularly on very significant projects where there's a lot of public concern, virtually.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: And we always appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: And it can be either on camera or even telephonically through the link.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: So it works nicely in those regards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: As far as the alternate timing, I would have to, I'm not sure what the requirements are, but I know that there are a lot of individual outreach

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: opportunities that the staff engages in through the borough offices for specific projects.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: And so those are, again, sort of what I was saying is meeting people where they want to be met or reaching them where they want to be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: Those are some ways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein
utterances.text: And that could be a really good way for council members to work with the department.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I just hope in your roles, in addition to us, because I do feel like it is also on us as council members, but I hope in your roles, too, that you push the department to better engage because the process has changed.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I think a lot of times, like, communities, people, they sort of, like, wait to use their political capital for when these projects come to the council.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But because these projects are not going to come to the council in the same way, that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: opportunity won't be there.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so I do think it is incumbent upon like all of us to figure out better ways to inform the community on how to best ensure that their voices are heard.

chapters.summary: Williams says DCP was under-resourced under Mayor Adams and that she used campaign funds for robocalls, nonprofits for education, and food to improve accessibility. She says community engagement is shortchanged and inequitable across communities.
chapters.title: Williams comments on DCP resources and her own engagement efforts

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And love DCP, love the people in the Queen's office, but you know, maybe this is a new administration, but under Mayor Adams, they were significantly under-resourced.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so I supplemented

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: doing robocalls using my campaign funds just because I wanted the community to know about, you know, our meetings and opportunities to engage.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I supplemented additional education to educate the community on the land use process by working with nonprofit organizations outside of DCP.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You know, I use my own funds to pay for food.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Like that is an accessibility thing as well for people who are coming in the evening.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so again,

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Love DCP, and I know that they end the Queen's office so much.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Shout-outs to Jasmine and, of course, Dan.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But I do feel like, you know, they have so much resources to do that type of work over the summer.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: We did door knocking, the council's community engagement unit.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thanks to Adrienne Adams, she allowed her community engagement unit to do door knocking in the summer.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But this is the council.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Technically supplementing what the agency was supposed to do, but because I was like passionate about making sure as many people as possible to the best of my abilities were aware, we did it.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But it is

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: and it is hard.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I just think sometimes we shortchange the community engagement piece, and that's the real harm, not necessarily whether or not we

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: do everything they say, but I feel like for certain communities, not all communities, because for certain communities, they have an already organized infrastructure locally, and they can...

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Quickly corral and have hundreds of people testify.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But for other communities that don't have that built-in infrastructure or resource, it is extremely hard to get them to participate.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I think it is a disservice to us in government to not truly hear the voices of the community when we're making these decisions.

chapters.summary: Williams asks what role the Council should continue to play in securing modifications, investments, and other benefits under the new land use processes.
chapters.title: Williams asks what role Council should play in securing benefits

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I'm going to skip one question and just say, what role, if any, should the council continue to play in securing benefits?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But to me, it's not always about benefits.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It's also about modifications to some of these projects.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: What role do you think we should play?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And you all had really good advice.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Maybe we should talk offline about figuring out how to make sure the council still plays an important role.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But we'd love to know on the record what role, if any, you think the council should continue to play in securing modifications, investments, and et cetera.

chapters.summary: Srinivasan says the Council role remains imperative. At LPC and BSA, which had no formal Council role, Council input was often incorporated; under ELURP and Fast Track, Council members can testify and maintain ongoing relationships with DCP. Private applicants are encouraged but not required to meet Council and community boards.
chapters.title: Meenakshi Srinivasan answers on Council role

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I think the council plays an incredibly important role.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And I just want to talk about my experience before when I chaired Landmarks and the PSA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Both boards had no formal, and the process had no formal role for the council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: But still, I think we were always open to hearing their position, and very often it was incorporated into the decisions that were made.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: So I think that even though we now have ELERP and Housing Fast Track, I think the role of the council is still imperative, and it can be...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: It can be sort of implemented either through the, I think, the formal process, which is at your public hearings where the commissioners will have a chance to hear your point of view and your written testimony,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: but also just this ongoing relationship with the department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And I think that's critical.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I worked in city planning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: We always worked with the council members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And yes, it's possible over time different administrations may have had different approaches.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: But I think that for big projects, significant projects, there is a role that...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: That starts even before the application is filed, and I would encourage the department to continue to do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I think in the case of private applications,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I think the department does encourage private applicants and their development team to meet with council members and community boards.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yes, encourage and require are two different things.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Because we know when they have to come to us because they come to us.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And then you do have those developers or really smart lobbyists that are proactive in their approach.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But that is not a requirement for them to do.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So it is very piecemeal.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And it differs across projects, lobbyists, whatever other advisors that they have with them, because it's, like you said, it's an encouragement.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It's not a requirement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: It's not a requirement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I don't believe there's any requirement that they have to do it that is prior to an application being filed or before a hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: But they're encouraged, and you're right, it varies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: But projects also vary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Some are small, some have a development team, which is very modest, and others will have, as you noted, an incredible team of people, and some of those actually have the resources to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: meet with council members and community boards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: In multiple venues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: But just to go back to this general question, I think that the role is, I would encourage council members and community boards to continue to express your opinions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And I think that the commission

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: has a duty to deliberate on that and consider modifications or other kinds of responses to those concerns.

chapters.title: Williams comments on sewer infrastructure and asks Crowell about Council input

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: so I'm gonna let her follow up on that but I just wanted to have an unlike question comment sorry chair I just wanted to comment on that you can reserve your question for when she asked is that

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so just, I'm very interested in that.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Question and how you all will make certain determinations around these projects that are not neighborhood plans.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So it might be lot to lot, which looks a lot different than, you know, a whole, you know, 30, 40, 50 block rezoning.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But to just stay on theme about the council's role and Mr.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Crowell,

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: seeing your hearing response makes complete sense based off of our conversation that we had, but you repeatedly, which I love,

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams

utterances.text: And how should commissioners weigh a local council member's position when it conflicts with citywide housing goals?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julie Stein

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you all and congratulations on your nominations.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Lee says her Queens district has four community boards, low density, flooding, and no subway. She asks what information commissioners need to determine whether existing infrastructure can support new development in the 12 low-production districts and fast-track projects.
chapters.title: Councilmember Lee questions panel on infrastructure adequacy in low-production districts

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Now I'm going to pass it off to Council Member Lee.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I was going to say deputy speaker.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: You should just ask.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: But she and I are very particularly interested in this answer because it impacts our areas of Queens pretty significantly.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Just so you know, I have...

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Four community boards in my district.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: It's very low density.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: She's laughing at me because we've had so many of these conversations.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And, you know, it is different.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so first I just want to recognize and appreciate the fact that you all are collectively saying that you want to

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: really listen to the community board and council member voices because I do believe as you said Mr.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Knuckles also before every district is very different in terms of its characteristic neighborhood what works for one may not work for another

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: but I think we've been experiencing especially with a lot of the flooding for example I'll just use that as an example in my district because

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Deputy Speaker and I, she used to have the part of Hollis before redistricting where the family had passed away because of the basement apartment that got flooded.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And it is now in my district.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And what happened recently is that because there's been so much flooding,

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: one of the houses literally fell off of its foundation and had to be demolished.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so it's been very challenging.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And just to give more context, I think DEP put a $20 million project tank underneath the ground to deal with this issue, and it clearly has not worked.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so...

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: You know, in the 12 communities or districts with the lowest production

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: in the previous five years, it requires that the commission make a determination as the quote-unquote adequacy of existing transportation, sewer, and other infrastructure before approval of a project.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And for projects reviewed through the fast-track affordable housing process,

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: What information would you need to determine whether existing infrastructure can support new development?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
