utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I have no trains, subways, nothing in my district.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So infrastructure is a big concern.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Across the street in your district, I got it, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: But, yeah, we have a lot of challenges there in terms of infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So I just wanted to know what those– what information you would need to determine whether the existing infrastructure can support new development.

chapters.summary: Crowell distinguishes larger projects with comprehensive environmental review from smaller projects with cumulative impacts. He says Council members can influence infrastructure through the budget and capital planning process outside land use.
chapters.title: Anthony Crowell answers on infrastructure review

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I think it's important to sort of disaggregate two types of projects we're talking about because there could be more significant applications that come in through this process that would come along with a really comprehensive environmental review.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: In those projects, you would have information about potential impacts and potential mitigations, and that is the information that we would rely on in order to evaluate the projects comprehensively.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I think this came up separately in one of the questions that Kenneth had responded to, but

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: there also is the potential for there to be more smaller projects that incrementally or cumulatively have impacts, but each individually do not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And this is a thing we've seen in the history of New York City overall, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Subway crowding, as an example, school crowding, as an example, each individual project doesn't have an impact on itself, but together they do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And I think this is going back to my earlier point where the land use process is not the end-all, be-all of planning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: These are places where the council members, in conversation with the administration and the capital planning process outside of land use, really you have a lot of influence over, you know, through the budget process where

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: investments can happen both in the short and long term to make sure that those incremental projects don't have a cumulatively negative impact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Or if they do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: they're being thought through with more comprehensive neighborhood investments.

chapters.summary: Lee asks whether there are city properties the city would not build on and how to balance the housing mandate with neighborhood characteristics. She asks for deeper criteria beyond project-by-project review.
chapters.title: Lee asks about city properties not to build on and balancing housing mandate

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Just out of curiosity, I wanted to kind of, as I was listening to all of you answer the other questions, I kind of wanted to flip it and just ask, are there any city properties that the city would not build on, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So how do you balance?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Your sort of roles to, you know, and your mandate to build housing, you know, while also balancing that in terms of the neighborhood characteristics and some of the other questions that the council members had.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Are you asking whether there are any proposals that we would reject or if there are any city properties that we believe nothing should be built on?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I guess both.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And I guess some, I mean, I know it's obviously a nuanced question in the sense that every project is different, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And some may, you know, not go forward for environmental reasons.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Others may not go forward because it's just not deemed possible to build there.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: But just wanting to get a little bit kind of building off my previous question a little bit more sort of a deeper dive into what the criteria is.

chapters.summary: Crowell says the mandate is not to stack people wherever possible but to create livable, attractive, affordable neighborhoods. He says orderly growth and neighborhood quality matter.
chapters.title: Anthony Crowell answers on livability and orderly growth

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: So I want to go back.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I can't now remember which council member mentioned this, but someone was speaking before about livability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I think it may have been Council Member Riley.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And how important it is not to just be building for affordability, but also livability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I think there's, you know, the potential to misinterpret the mandate as a we just want to stack people on top of each other wherever we can house them versus we want to have orderly growth in New York City where we're continuing to be

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: a collection of neighborhoods where people really want to live.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And I think obviously, you know, goes towards the latter and that, you know, we're not just thinking about where can you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Warehouse people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: It's how can we build neighborhoods that create attractive, affordable locations where individuals and families can thrive now and into the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: So it doesn't answer your question directly, but I think that is the philosophy.

chapters.summary: Lee describes her district as mostly R1 and R2 with no trains and asks how to balance housing needs with neighborhood concerns beyond hearing community input.
chapters.title: Lee asks about balancing housing needs in low-density neighborhoods

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And I guess if I were to ask a different, so when considering the proposals that increase housing, especially in lower density neighborhoods like mine, because I have mostly R1 and R2.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Some are three, almost little to no are four and above.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so just to give you a sense of how low density it is, and my predecessor used to joke that on the subway map, the key slash legend of the subway map is right on top of my district because there's literally nothing there

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: in terms of trains and railroads and everything.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So when you consider those types of lower density neighborhoods, how would you balance the housing needs with the neighborhood concerns?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I think a lot of it you have alluded to, which is hearing the community's responses and taking that into consideration.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: But what other factors?

chapters.summary: Knuckles says low-density areas should look for non-residential land, manufacturing, industrial, and commercial strips that can accommodate appropriately scaled mixed-use development. Every community should play a role while respecting neighborhood character.
chapters.title: Kenneth Knuckles answers on opportunities in low-density areas

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: At least for me, I would want to know, and I would expect, frankly, that...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: This kind of diligence would have been done by whoever's proposing a project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Where is the land that can be converted to residential that's not currently residential?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: You know, where is your manufacturing properties?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Probably not many of them, but certainly there should be some.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Portion of them, industrial properties, commercial strips that can accommodate appropriately scaled mixed-use development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I think

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Those are realistically the opportunities in low-density areas such as yours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Because, you know, I don't think anyone on the commission is insensitive to the nature and character of a given neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: We all cherish our neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: But as a part of...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: everyone, every community playing its appropriate role.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I think we've got to look at areas that historically have not been

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: the source of residential development, but arguably can be in this new and enlightened

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: era we were in.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Yeah, no, and I appreciated your answer before to Councilmember Riley's question alluding to that, so I appreciate that.

chapters.summary: Lee notes that small projects are expensive and asks Margaret Anadu about public-private partnerships to make five-, ten-, or twenty-unit affordable projects viable in low-density areas.
chapters.title: Lee asks Margaret Anadu about making small affordable projects viable

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And I sort of wanted to answer or ask a question more to Margaret, but want to open it up to everyone.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So first of all, I appreciate your laughing emoji in your testimony, which I appreciate because I do those all the time.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: To your point that you just brought up with where to look, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: For example, I do have a couple commercial corridors, right, where it's just one floor of commercial space.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So, but one of the things that I always used to talk to DCP about is that it's just so expensive to build.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Like lower numbers of units.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so I've always asked the question, because I can tell you certain places,

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: even in my areas where perhaps without, you know, disrupting the neighborhood makeup, you can still build maybe five units here, 10 units here, 20 here, and it adds up right throughout the districts.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so I'm just wondering if

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: you know, especially Margaret, because I love how you talk about the public-private partnership, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And are there ways that we can partner so that it's not as expensive to build for something?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Because I don't think a developer would go in saying, hey, we want to build five units of affordable housing here.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Because it's not financially viable for them.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so how do we make it less expensive to build in certain neighborhoods where maybe we can add a little bit everywhere, right, to address the crisis, the housing crisis?

chapters.summary: Anadu says development in New York is expensive but small projects can work, citing Myrtle Avenue and Fulton Street. Assembling lots can create efficiency while maintaining neighborhood scale, and a little housing everywhere is worthwhile.
chapters.title: Margaret Anadu answers on incremental housing and small projects

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I love that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Thank you for asking it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I think one thing I'd say, and I hope this doesn't sound...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: pessimistic, but I mean it just as framing like development in New York is expensive, big, small, inefficient, less, it just is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: So you sort of start from a premise of hard and kind of go with what makes it quite frankly less hard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: And I think there are actually like really great examples around the city of rezoning if you look at, you know,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Myrtle Avenue in northwest Brooklyn, which was a lot of, you know, single lots where there's now ability for, you know, increased density of housing above.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: And you had folks who put together, you know, four and five single lots.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: And then it makes more sense.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: It's still not going to be three and four hundred.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: units, but you start to get to a little bit more efficiency and still maintain neighborhood scale and character.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Also similar work you've seen on Fulton Street through parts of Bedford-Stuyvesant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: So I think the idea that because something is not going to be a

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: a skyscraper or hundreds of units that it's not sort of worthwhile in smaller projects over time, I think is false.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I feel like one of the ideas that I've been excited about in terms of just housing lately is this idea of just sometimes it's a little bit everywhere.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: And I think there's a conversation that pushes that to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I think, what did you say, warehousing people, just stacking people everywhere where it's not that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: It's really sort of what additional housing is possible in context, in character, with the right infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: And I think if that's five units over here and five units over here, I think that's still incredibly worthwhile, even if it is potentially less efficient.

chapters.summary: Crowell says growth will look different in different neighborhoods and zoning can create value for small projects. He says housing growth also serves residents who want to stay, children returning, and people downsizing.
chapters.title: Anthony Crowell answers on incremental growth and local housing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, just to piggyback on what you mentioned, there is an opportunity for incremental growth, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Growth in your neighborhood is going to look very different than in Councilmember Rue's neighborhood, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Like, there are just, context is really important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: But one of the opportunities through zoning is to create more value that makes these developments more attractive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And so I think one of the things to look at is where can we make, you know, appropriate changes, appropriate changes that will both

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: create more citywide housing, but also housing opportunities for people who are in your neighborhood who want to stay in your neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: The children who grew up in the neighborhood who want to come back, people who are retiring and want to downsize.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I think there's this sort of like...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: False dichotomy, the idea that if a neighborhood accommodates housing growth, it's only for citywide concerns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I think we really also have a lot of people who wish they could stay where they grew up and actually have a lot of challenge finding housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: So a lot of the tools that come along at CPC, we are evaluating the opportunity to find a little bit of value in neighborhoods where a little bit more housing might all of a sudden become attractive.

chapters.summary: Srinivasan says City of Yes allows modest density and ADUs in low-density areas, and 2025 charter amendments aim to address incentives for large out-of-scale rezonings. She says rezonings are tailored to communities and sensitive to lower-density areas.
chapters.title: Meenakshi Srinivasan answers on City of Yes and charter changes

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I just wanted to add that there are a couple of things that are in play which may sort of change the landscape.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I think one is that the city of Yes, which was a little housing everywhere, that concept has been implemented.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And we'll see.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I know there are concerns and people have different points of view.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: But what it basically did, particularly in lower density neighborhoods, it allowed for a little more housing through ADUs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And then also just increases in density, which were fairly modest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: But the other thing is even the charter provisions or the amendments that were adopted in 2025, which talks about these modest increases, is also trying to address that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: The incentives that allowed people to go into neighborhoods and propose rezonings were always large and out of scale.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And the smaller projects never really got off the ground.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: So I think it'll be interesting to see that with this charter change, what kind of applications come before the commission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I would also just say that, and I think all of us know this, that...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: That rezonings are tailored to a particular community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: It's not the same in one neighborhood versus another, and I think there's a lot of sensitivity to lower-density neighborhoods and how best to accommodate growth.

chapters.summary: Lee says her district's low density had legitimate reasons and cites the Creedmoor state property project. She says community engagement produced a middle ground with housing, veterans and senior affordable housing, homeownership, schools, and a firehouse.
chapters.title: Lee comments on Creedmoor project and community engagement

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And to your point that

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: You made earlier, Anthony, that's, you know, my area of Queens is where, you know, they really were fighting to sort of, because, you know, there's, again, every area of the city is different.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And in that particular area, because of the zoning and the neighborhood of the housing that's there,

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: there were reasons, legit reasons, why they kept it lower density versus other areas.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so I appreciated you saying that.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: But just one final thing I'll just say is that, you know, there is an example of a housing project in my district, which hasn't happened yet, but it's on state property.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: It's not city property.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: But to all of your points, where can you look to build?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: It's on the property of Creedmoor, which is going to be a 50-acre project, which is huge.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And this is an example of where I think really working hand in hand with the community paid off in the sense that, you know, everyone may not have gotten exactly what they wanted on either side, but it came to a good middle ground area.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Because I think the...

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: That property had been discussed for 40, 50 years, and the community board and the civic leaders and folks were okay with it in the end because there really was

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: a lot of listening that happened to the community's concerns and how do you adapt that into the project.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: You know, I'm actually, you know, glad that we were able to get it to a good place.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And it's going to be everything.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: from housing, veterans housing, senior affordable housing, affordable homeownership, which I feel like is not talked about enough, right, in certain communities.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And just, you know, same thing that we talked about before, schools, probably a firehouse that is going to be needed there.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So it was a very well thought out process.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so I hope that that's something we can continue to model in certain neighborhoods in particular.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: But yes, thank you.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Brewer says she has done over 200 ULURPs and that the Council role is important. She is angry that Board 7 is among the 12 low-production districts and asks how affordable housing can be built in historic districts and whether commissioners will oppose the mayor.
chapters.title: Councilmember Brewer questions panel on historic districts and affordable housing

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn it over to Council Member Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I've done about over 200 ULERPs.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I have to say that in my experience, the city council's role is incredibly important.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I was able to get a whole park, a new school, and I could go on and on.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And just recently, even with Community Board 4, which is probably the most sophisticated community board in the city,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: regarding affordable housing, we were able to get more affordable housing in an MIH, more than the MIH.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I'm worried.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Board 7 is one of your 12, and I'm pissed about it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Love to go to court about it, to be honest with you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm so angry.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And we want affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Years and years.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: No, no, Gail.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We're going to go to the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Land is cheaper.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We're not going to give you a voucher.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We're not going to do affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And nobody who is going to build wants affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They all want condos.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: $23 million a pop, each condo.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So it's a whole different world than...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So my question to you is, in situations like that, where we want affordable housing, we have SROs now that are being converted, but that doesn't count because they're not new.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You only count new for the 12.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You have to have a new place.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And we're the second most dense neighborhood in the city, I assume in the country.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I don't think there's one blade of grass that's available on the Upper West Side for new housing, unless you tear housing down.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So my question is, well, how do you handle historic districts?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Would you tear down housing in historic districts?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And how do you think affordable housing can be built in a district like ours that isn't convertible?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I didn't think, you know, I've got two vacant SROs, 57th Street and 79th Street, and I can't get the city to make them or buy them or do something with a nonprofit.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Too expensive, can't do it, won't do it, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I don't know where we're supposed to get affordable housing if to convert, I mean, to...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Get around this 12.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So my question is a historic district, and what do you do in a district like ours to change the situation?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And also, will you go against the mayor, even though you're appointed by him, on some of these issues?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's my other question.

chapters.summary: Anadu says the low-production designation can feel punitive but reflects economic realities such as expensive land and few lots. She says fast-track can reduce cost and risk if robust community engagement remains.
chapters.title: Margaret Anadu answers on low-production designation and costs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Thank you for that and just all your service and passion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I think, and I hope I'm not speaking out of school here, but I feel like some of the sort of designation of the lowest 12, it almost feels like it's punitive or, you know, that these districts have done something wrong or, you know,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: or made a mistake, but one of the things you outlined, even in talking about developers, talking about land in the Bronx versus land in your district, it just highlights one of the, you know, for example, economic realities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: You've seen a lot more affordable housing developed in parts of the cities, especially private, on private lots where it's cheaper.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: So I just wanted to share two things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: One,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I hope it's a really just healthy opportunity to talk in real terms around what are some of the reasons why some districts have produced less housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: That seems like a really great practical one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: It's mostly developed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: There are less lots.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: It's more expensive to do so because, you know, it's in one of the most highest expensive land parts of the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: So I view that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: As a positive to highlight and have people, stakeholders, commission, community members, et cetera, people understand what it takes to create affordable housing and what are just objectively some of the barriers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: So I look at that positively.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: I think two,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: part of that and I just I always think about that just the capitalization of these things and what makes it feasible

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Part of the fast track from my perspective, and this comes with optimism, that we can still have robust and significant and real and genuine community engagement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: If you take that as a premise, which I do, then I view it as just a way to make the process more efficient.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: And therefore less expensive, and therefore less risky, and therefore lower the cost of capital, which to me feels like it could be part of a solution to some of the things you've highlighted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: Like it's just more expensive in your district.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Margaret Anadu
utterances.text: So I'm actually hopeful that as opposed to it being perceived as this kind of punitive designation, that it becomes one that both gets everyone more educated and hopefully actually just makes the...

chapters.summary: Brewer says her district is highly educated and votes heavily, doubts the housing goals can be met, and again asks about historic districts, saying LPC is no good.
chapters.title: Brewer responds on her district and historic districts

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I don't think you could educate my district anymore.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: There's nobody in that district who needs education.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I don't mean your district.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I meant the whole city.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, because we're, they are, you know, people vote 20 times more than any other district in the city.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Number one in the country.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Just assuming you know that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I just think it's a hard, I don't know what we're going to, we're not going to be able to accomplish what is desired.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And also, what do you think about historic districts?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I feel strongly that they should not be torn down.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But that seems to be what some people want to do.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And don't rely on LPC because they're no good.

chapters.summary: Srinivasan says historic district protections remain and creative approaches can allow housing in historic districts without demolition, citing Soho, Noho, and Tribeca projects. Brewer says they may disagree.
chapters.title: Meenakshi Srinivasan answers on historic districts and housing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: You tickled my answer, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: But I think protections that are in historic districts remain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: This concern that you'll find wholesale, I don't know, demolition of buildings and buildings that are going to be out of scale to address the housing crisis, I don't think that's going to happen.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: 500 Columbus Avenue right now, that's what's happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that particular project, but I definitely will take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: But I think the idea in historic districts now sort of coming up against housing, sometimes I think it does be like the commission should...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: Think about this creatively and there may be new responses to how we deal with historic districts than in the past.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: because of this housing crisis, I don't think that means that we should take away historic districts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: I don't think it means we should tear down buildings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: But I think there are ways that historic districts can produce housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And I've seen that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: When I was the chair, there were housing projects in Soho and Noho, and they're all to scale.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And similarly in Tribeca.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: So there's a way to allow development to take place in historic districts without actually taking away the historic.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You and I may disagree on that one, but okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: We may.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Yeah, we will.

chapters.summary: Knuckles, a fellow Dinkins alumnus, offers to meet with Brewer and city officials to identify affordable housing opportunities on the Upper West Side. He says consensus on the need for affordable housing should allow consensus on sites.
chapters.title: Kenneth Knuckles and Brewer discuss Upper West Side opportunities

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Anybody else?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Hello, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Hello, sir.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How are you?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I know you very well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: We're fellow Dinkins alumni, among other things.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We're both old.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I would hope that some contingent of the department and city government could sit down with you and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: look at and discuss where you think opportunities are for affordable housing that are not being

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: currently focused upon or looked at.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Because, I mean, you've laid it out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: The Upper West Side is cheap jowl.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: You know, there are no large lots except where, you know, certain developers are putting up, you know, super, super high buildings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: So, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Gail, if you don't mind me calling you Gail.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Gail's fine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: You know the bricks and mortar as well as anybody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I would just like, I just think personally, you know, I would like to sit with you and get your views on where.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: There are opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Maybe we agree, maybe we disagree.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: But if we all want affordable housing, there's no disagreement about the need for affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: So if there's a consensus on that issue,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: then I think we ought to be able to find some consensus around some sites.

chapters.summary: Brewer cites the ABC site, 2.4 acres, where Excel wants a building bigger than the Empire State Building with only 7 percent affordable off-site and mostly senior units. She says the city must do things differently in well-resourced districts.
chapters.title: Brewer cites ABC site and Excel project

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Well, right now we have the ABC site, 2.4 acres, and Excel wants to put up a building bigger than the Empire State Building, and only 7% affordable and off-site and seniors mostly, which we don't want.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's all tough, and you have to do things differently, and the administration has to have, you know, it's really easy to rack up apartments in other parts of the city.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But when you have good schools, good transportation, and you want diversity, you have to do things differently.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have not seen anybody do that.

chapters.summary: Crowell asks to join the meeting with Brewer and says he understands the bottom-12 concerns. He says commissioners must decide based on evidence, not political influence, and that no one has pressured him in four years. Brewer thanks the panel.
chapters.title: Anthony Crowell answers on independence; Brewer thanks panel

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Hi, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Nice to see you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I just want to concur with Ken, and I would love to be in that meeting if I may invite myself, because I think that's really valuable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I've questioned the what-ifs with the bottom 12, so I understand the concern.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I certainly understand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: the contours of your district very well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And I think that Ken's suggestion is a prudent one, given the moment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: You had asked another question about being independent on the commission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And I think that it's imperative that all of us take the information that we have before us, whatever

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: the applications, the studies, the analyses, all the public testimony we hear, and make our determinations based on that, not on political influence, regardless of whether it's from the mayor or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And so I think that's...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That hasn't always happened in the past, so that would be nice if it happened in the future.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It has not.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And this is a fine mayor, but he doesn't know anything about housing or development.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: He knows other things.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And so you have to really be independent and think about differently.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: He knows other things, but not that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I can say, just for what it's worth, since I've been on the commission for four years, no one has ever called me to say to me, you should vote this way, you need to vote this way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I've always been given the space to do my independent analysis and to come down.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Based on the totality of what I've seen and the different evolutions of applications and projects that I've seen.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And I will continue to do that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Anybody else?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Ung asks what role environmental justice should play in the commission's work. Srinivasan says environmental review now includes environmental justice analysis. Crowell says environmental justice neighborhoods also need access to process and public input, especially disenfranchised residents.
chapters.title: Chair Ung asks about environmental justice in CPC work

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I see just a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: We will be concluding today.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So to environmental review and justice, what role should environmental justice play in the commission's work?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Anyone, or more than one, feel free.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: My understanding, well, projects that go through the environmental review are now required, I believe, to look at environmental justice as a standalone sort of analysis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: So I think that takes care of it at one angle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: And I think that, you know, in terms of the commission otherwise looking at projects which don't have an environmental review, then I think it's similar to other kinds of comments that we may hear during the public review process and to see if

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Meenakshi Srinivasan
utterances.text: there are ways to address it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I've had the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: Thank you so much for this question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I think it's really critical.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: I've had the opportunity over my career to work in many environmental justice neighborhoods and know very acutely the concerns that come along with them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And I think the other thing I would say in addition to what Manakshi mentioned is that there also can be a relationship between sort of access to process in an environmental neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And so I think it would be particularly important when we're talking about a neighborhood that has had environmental harms in the past to also make sure that enough is being done for public input because maybe

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: some of the most disenfranchised New Yorkers may be living in environmental justice communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: And I know that there is an incredible network of nonprofits and community organizations that do work in these neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Crowell
utterances.text: But I think we would look in particular towards making sure we're hearing the perspectives of individuals that are impacted by a project, whether it's through those organizations or making sure they're coming out to testify.

chapters.summary: Chair Ung asks how environmental review should inform CPC decision-making. Knuckles says it determines undue impacts on water, sewer, open space, and air quality and remains necessary even when SEQRA is not required. Srinivasan says CEQR identifies impacts, alternatives, and mitigation; Stein says it helps assess infrastructure sufficiency.
chapters.title: Chair Ung asks about purpose of environmental review and decision-making

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: As a follow-up, the Commission, as you said, oversees implementation of SEEKER.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: How do you see that as the purpose of your mental review, and how should it inform the Commission's decision-making?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Chair, would you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The Commission oversees implementation of SEEKER.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I hope I'm saying this right.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: What do you see as the purpose of the environmental review and how should it inform the Commission's decision-making?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Well, I think the purpose is clear in terms of determining whether or not a project will unduly

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: and unfavorably impact a community in terms of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: water, sewer, open space, environmental issues, air quality, etc.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Those are issues that are, I believe, determinative of whether or not

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: a project can and should proceed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: That critique, of course, comes to us principally through our department staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: And where, in those instances where it will not be required,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: And first of all, you know, that the determination ultimately was based upon the fact that a large percentage of projects that came before the commission

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: did not have negative impacts as it relates to SECRA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Now, you know, one can always argue about that, but...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: The fact that that that secret may not be required does not

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: at all relieve us of the responsibility of assessing the environmental impact of a project on on on the.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: Given community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: That does not cease.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: And as I've said probably about 20 times, I think our role is heightened in those instances where SECRA is not necessarily required to nonetheless

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles
utterances.text: ensure at least to an

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Knuckles

summary: The Committee on Rules, Privileges, Elections, Standards and Ethics held a hearing on six nominations: Martha King to the New York City Board of Correction and five City Planning Commission appointments or reappointments.

Martha King testified about her BOC experience, jail oversight, deaths in custody, solitary confinement, mental health, borough-based jails, and ICE/sanctuary issues, then answered questions from Council members.

Five CPC nominees—Anthony Crowell, Kenneth Knuckles, Julie Stein, Margaret Anadu, and Meenakshi Srinivasan—gave opening statements and answered questions on housing, infrastructure, community benefits, ELURP, environmental review, and Council/community engagement; no public speakers testified.
